entries.2b4eb58cf20eecdc49497099356413cd09d6bcdb: <div sID="gen10267" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="41" osisID="Job.41" sID="Job.41"/> <div eID="gen10267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10268" type="x-p"/> The description here given of the leviathan, a very large, strong, formidable fish, or water-animal, is designed yet further to convince Job of his own impotency, and of God's omnipotence, that he might be humbled for his folly in making so bold with him as he had done. I. To convince Job of his own weakness he is here challenged to subdue and tame this leviathan if he can, and make himself master of him (<reference osisRef="Job.41.1-Job.41.9">ver. 1-9</reference>), and, since he cannot do this, he must own himself utterly unable to stand before the great God, <reference osisRef="Job.41.10">ver. 10</reference>. II. To convince Job of God's power and terrible majesty several particular instances are here given of the strength and terror of the leviathan, which is no more than what God has given him, nor more than he has under his check, <reference osisRef="Job.41.11-Job.41.12">ver. 11, 12</reference>. The face of the leviathan is here described to be terrible (<reference osisRef="Job.41.12">ver. 12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.41.14">14</reference>), his scales close (<reference osisRef="Job.41.15-Job.41.17">ver. 15-17</reference>), his breath and neesings sparkling (<reference osisRef="Job.41.18-Job.41.21">ver. 18-21</reference>), his flesh firm (<reference osisRef="Job.41.22-Job.41.24">ver. 22-24</reference>), his strength and spirit, when he is attacked, insuperable (<reference osisRef="Job.41.25-Job.41.30">ver. 25-30</reference>), his motions turbulent, and disturbing to the waters (<reference osisRef="Job.41.31-Job.41.32">ver. 31, 32</reference>), so that, upon the whole, he is a very terrible creature, and man is no match for him, <reference osisRef="Job.41.33-Job.41.34">ver. 33, 34</reference>.
entries.ff57f6196c35aa31c85a333d63bafa0471d67630: <div eID="gen10268" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Description of Leviathan. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen10269" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Canst thou draw out leviathan with a hook? or his tongue with a cord <hi type="italic">which</hi> thou lettest down? <hi type="super">2</hi> Canst thou put a hook into his nose? or bore his jaw through with a thorn? <hi type="super">3</hi> Will he make many supplications unto thee? will he speak soft <hi type="italic">words</hi> unto thee? <hi type="super">4</hi> Will he make a covenant with thee? wilt thou take him for a servant for ever? <hi type="super">5</hi> Wilt thou play with him as <hi type="italic">with</hi> a bird? or wilt thou bind him for thy maidens? <hi type="super">6</hi> Shall the companions make a banquet of him? shall they part him among the merchants? <hi type="super">7</hi> Canst thou fill his skin with barbed irons? or his head with fish spears? <hi type="super">8</hi> Lay thine hand upon him, remember the battle, do no more. <hi type="super">9</hi> Behold, the hope of him is in vain: shall not <hi type="italic">one</hi> be cast down even at the sight of him? <hi type="super">10</hi> None <hi type="italic">is so</hi> fierce that dare stir him up: who then is able to stand before me? <div eID="gen10269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10270" type="x-p"/> Whether this leviathan be a whale or a crocodile is a great dispute among the learned, which I will not undertake to determine; some of the particulars agree more easily to the one, others to the other; both are very strong and fierce, and the power of the Creator appears in them. The ingenious Sir Richard Blackmore, though he admits the more received opinion concerning the <hi type="italic">behemoth,</hi> that it must be meant of the <hi type="italic">elephant,</hi> yet agrees with the learned Bochart's notion of the <hi type="italic">leviathan,</hi> that it is the <hi type="italic">crocodile,</hi> which was so well known in the river of Egypt. I confess that that which inclines me rather to understand it of the whale is not only because it is much larger and a nobler animal, but because, in the history of the Creation, there is such an express notice taken of it as is not of any other species of animals whatsoever (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.21">Gen. i. 21</reference>, <hi type="italic">God created great whales</hi>), by which it appears, not only that whales were well known in those parts in the time of Moses, who lived a little after Job, but that the creation of whales was generally looked upon as a most illustrious proof of the eternal power and godhead of the Creator; and we may conjecture that this was the reason (for otherwise it seems unaccountable) why Moses there so particularly mentions the creation of the whales, because God had so lately insisted upon the bulk and strength of that creature than of any other, as the proof of his power; and the <hi type="italic">leviathan</hi> is here spoken of as an inhabitant of the sea (<reference osisRef="Job.41.31">v. 31</reference>), which the crocodile is not; and <reference osisRef="Ps.104.25-Ps.104.26">Ps. civ. 25, 26</reference>, <hi type="italic">there</hi> in <hi type="italic">the great and wide sea, is that leviathan.</hi> Here in these verses, <div eID="gen10270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10271" type="x-p"/> I. He shows how unable Job was to master the leviathan. 1. That he could not catch him, as a little fish, with angling, <reference osisRef="Job.41.1-Job.41.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. He had no bait wherewith to deceive him, no hook wherewith to catch him, no fish-line wherewith to draw him out of the water, nor a thorn to run through his gills, on which to carry him home. 2. That he could not make him his prisoner, nor force him to cry for quarter, or surrender himself at discretion, <reference osisRef="Job.41.3-Job.41.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. "He knows his own strength too well to <hi type="italic">make many supplications to thee,</hi> and to <hi type="italic">make a covenant with thee</hi> to be thy servant on condition thou wilt save his life." 3. That he could not entice him into a cage, and keep him there as a bird for the children to play with, <reference osisRef="Job.41.5">v. 5</reference>. There are creatures so little, so weak, as to be easily restrained thus, and triumphed over; but the leviathan is not one of these: he is made to be the terror, not the sport and diversion, of mankind. 4. That he could not have him served up to his table; he and his companions could not make a banquet of him; his flesh is too strong to be fit for food, and, if it were not, he is not easily caught. 5. That they could not enrich themselves with the spoil of him: <hi type="italic">Shall they part him among the merchants,</hi> the bones to one, the oil to another? If they can catch him, they will; but it is probable that the art of fishing for whales was not brought to perfection then, as it has been since. 6. That they could not destroy him, could not <hi type="italic">fill his head with fish-spears,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.41.7">v. 7</reference>. He kept out of the reach of their instruments of slaughter, or, if they touched him, they could not touch him to the quick. 7. That it was to no purpose to attempt it: <hi type="italic">The hope of</hi> taking <hi type="italic">him is in vain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.41.9">v. 9</reference>. If men go about to seize him, so formidable is he that the very sight of him will appal them, and make a stout man ready to faint away: <hi type="italic">Shall not one be cast down even at the sight of him?</hi> and will not that deter the pursuers from their attempt? Job is told, at his peril, to <hi type="italic">lay his hand upon him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.41.8">v. 8</reference>. "Touch him if thou dare; <hi type="italic">remember the battle,</hi> how unable thou art to encounter such a force, and what is therefore likely to be the issue of the battle, <hi type="italic">and do no more,</hi> but desist from the attempt." It is good to remember the battle before we engage in a war, and put off the harness in time if we foresee it will be to no purpose to gird it on. Job is hereby admonished not to proceed in his controversy with God, but to make his peace with him, remembering what the battle will certainly end in if he come to an engagement. See <reference osisRef="Isa.27.4-Isa.27.5">Isa. xxvii. 4, 5</reference>. <div eID="gen10271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10272" type="x-p"/> II. Thence he infers how unable he was to contend with the Almighty. <hi type="italic">None is so fierce,</hi> none so fool-hardy, <hi type="italic">that he dares</hi> to <hi type="italic">stir up</hi> the leviathan (<reference osisRef="Job.41.10">v. 10</reference>), it being known that he will certainly be too hard for them; and <hi type="italic">who then is able to stand before God,</hi> either to impeach and arraign his proceedings or to out-face the power of his wrath? If the inferior creatures that are put under the feet of man, and over whom he has dominion, keep us in awe thus, how terrible must the majesty of our great Lord be, who has a sovereign dominion over us and against whom man has been so long in rebellion! <hi type="italic">Who can stand before him when once he is angry?</hi>
entries.78de9c45e94d2e85b82a467335266f852190a056: <div eID="gen10272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10273" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> Who hath prevented me, that I should repay <hi type="italic">him? whatsoever is</hi> under the whole heaven is mine. <hi type="super">12</hi> I will not conceal his parts, nor his power, nor his comely proportion. <hi type="super">13</hi> Who can discover the face of his garment? <hi type="italic">or</hi> who can come <hi type="italic">to him</hi> with his double bridle? <hi type="super">14</hi> Who can open the doors of his face? his teeth <hi type="italic">are</hi> terrible round about. <hi type="super">15</hi> <hi type="italic">His</hi> scales <hi type="italic">are his</hi> pride, shut up together <hi type="italic">as with</hi> a close seal. <hi type="super">16</hi> One is so near to another, that no air can come between them. <hi type="super">17</hi> They are joined one to another, they stick together, that they cannot be sundered. <hi type="super">18</hi> By his neesings a light doth shine, and his eyes <hi type="italic">are</hi> like the eyelids of the morning. <hi type="super">19</hi> Out of his mouth go burning lamps, <hi type="italic">and</hi> sparks of fire leap out. <hi type="super">20</hi> Out of his nostrils goeth smoke, as <hi type="italic">out</hi> of a seething pot or caldron. <hi type="super">21</hi> His breath kindleth coals, and a flame goeth out of his mouth. <hi type="super">22</hi> In his neck remaineth strength, and sorrow is turned into joy before him. <hi type="super">23</hi> The flakes of his flesh are joined together: they are firm in themselves; they cannot be moved. <hi type="super">24</hi> His heart is as firm as a stone; yea, as hard as a piece of the nether <hi type="italic">millstone.</hi> 25 When he raiseth up himself, the mighty are afraid: by reason of breakings they purify themselves. <hi type="super">26</hi> The sword of him that layeth at him cannot hold: the spear, the dart, nor the habergeon. <hi type="super">27</hi> He esteemeth iron as straw, <hi type="italic">and</hi> brass as rotten wood. <hi type="super">28</hi> The arrow cannot make him flee: slingstones are turned with him into stubble. <hi type="super">29</hi> Darts are counted as stubble: he laugheth at the shaking of a spear. <hi type="super">30</hi> Sharp stones <hi type="italic">are</hi> under him: he spreadeth sharp pointed things upon the mire. <hi type="super">31</hi> He maketh the deep to boil like a pot: he maketh the sea like a pot of ointment. <hi type="super">32</hi> He maketh a path to shine after him; <hi type="italic">one</hi> would think the deep <hi type="italic">to be</hi> hoary. <hi type="super">33</hi> Upon earth there is not his like, who is made without fear. <hi type="super">34</hi> He beholdeth all high <hi type="italic">things:</hi> he <hi type="italic">is</hi> a king over all the children of pride. <div eID="gen10273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10274" type="x-p"/> God, having in the <reference osisRef="Job.42.1-Job.42.6">foregoing verses</reference> shown Job how unable he was to deal with the leviathan, here sets forth his own power in that massy mighty creature. Here is, <div eID="gen10274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10275" type="x-p"/> I. God's sovereign dominion and independency laid down, <reference osisRef="Job.41.11">v. 11</reference>. 1. That he is indebted to none of his creatures. If any pretend he is indebted to them, let them make their demand and prove their debt, and they shall receive it in full and not by composition: "<hi type="italic">Who has prevented me?</hi>" that is, "who has laid any obligations upon me by any services he has done me? Who can pretend to be before-hand with me? If any were, I would not long be behind-hand with them; I would soon repay them." The apostle quotes this for the silencing of all flesh in God's presence, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.35">Rom. xi. 35</reference>. <hi type="italic">Who hath first given to him, and it shall be recompensed to him again?</hi> As God does not inflict upon us the evils we have deserved, so he does bestow upon us the favours we have not deserved. 2. That he is the rightful Lord and owner of all the creatures: "<hi type="italic">Whatsoever is under the whole heaven,</hi> animate or inanimate, <hi type="italic">is mine</hi> (and particularly this leviathan), at my command and disposal, what I have an incontestable property in and dominion over." All is his; we are his, all we have and do; and therefore we cannot make God our debtor; but <hi type="italic">of thy own, Lord, have we given thee.</hi> All is his, and therefore, if he were indebted to any, he has wherewithal to repay them; the debt is in good hands. All is his, and therefore he needs not our services, nor can he be benefited by them. <hi type="italic">If I were hungry I would not tell thee, for the world is mine and the fulness thereof,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.50.12">Ps. l. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen10275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10276" type="x-p"/> II. The proof and illustration of it, from the wonderful structure of the leviathan, <reference osisRef="Job.41.12">v. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen10276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10277" type="x-p"/> 1. The parts of his body, the power he exerts, especially when he is set upon, and the comely proportion of the whole of him, are what God will not conceal, and therefore what we must observe and acknowledge the power of God in. Though he is a creature of monstrous bulk, yet there is in him a <hi type="italic">comely proportion.</hi> In our eye beauty lies in that which is small (<hi type="italic">inest sua gratia parvis</hi>—<hi type="italic">little things have a gracefulness all their own</hi>) because we ourselves are so; but in God's eye even the leviathan is comely; and, if he pronounce even the whale, even the crocodile, so, it is not for us to say of any of the works of his hands that they are ugly or ill-favoured; it is enough to say so, as we have cause, of our own works. God here goes about to give us an anatomical view (as it were) of the leviathan; for his works appear most beautiful and excellent, and his wisdom and power appear most in them, when they are taken in pieces and viewed in their several parts and proportions. (1.) The leviathan, even <hi type="italic">prima facie</hi>—<hi type="italic">at first sight,</hi> appears formidable and inaccessible, <reference osisRef="Job.41.13-Job.41.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. Who dares come so near him while he is alive as to discover or take a distinct view of <hi type="italic">the face of the garment,</hi> the skin with which he is clothed as with a garment, so near him as to bridle him like a horse and so lead him away, so near him as to be within reach of his jaws, which are like <hi type="italic">a double bridle?</hi> Who will venture to look into his mouth, as we do into a horse's mouth? He that <hi type="italic">opens the doors of his face</hi> will see <hi type="italic">his teeth terrible round about,</hi> strong and sharp, and fitted to devour; it would make a man tremble to think of having a leg or an arm between them. (2.) <hi type="italic">His scales are</hi> his beauty and strength, and therefore <hi type="italic">his pride,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.41.15-Job.41.17">v. 15-17</reference>. The crocodile is indeed remarkable for his scales; if we understand it of the whale, we must understand by these <hi type="italic">shields</hi> (for so the word is) the several coats of his skin; or there might be whales in that country with scales. That which is remarkable concerning the scales is that <hi type="italic">they stick</hi> so close <hi type="italic">together,</hi> by which he is not only kept warm, for no air can pierce him, but kept safe, for no sword can pierce him through those scales. Fishes, that live in the water, are fortified accordingly by the wisdom of Providence, which gives clothes as it gives cold. (3.) He scatters terror with his very breath and looks; if he sneeze or spout up water, it is like a light shining, either with the froth or the light of the sun shining through it, <reference osisRef="Job.41.18">v. 18</reference>. The eyes of the whale are reported to shine in the night-time like a flame, or, as here, <hi type="italic">like the eye-lids of the morning;</hi> the same they say of the crocodile. The breath of this creature is so hot and fiery, from the great natural heat within, that <hi type="italic">burning lamps and sparks of fire,</hi> smoke and a flame, are said to <hi type="italic">go out of his mouth,</hi> even such as one would think sufficient to set coals on fire, <reference osisRef="Job.41.19-Job.41.21">v. 19-21</reference>. Probably these hyperbolical expressions are used concerning the leviathan to intimate the terror of the wrath of God, for that is it which all this is designed to convince us of. <hi type="italic">Fire out of his mouth devours,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.18.7-Ps.18.8">Ps. xviii. 7, 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">The breath of the Almighty,</hi> like a <hi type="italic">stream of brimstone, kindles Tophet,</hi> and will for ever keep it burning, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.33">Isa. xxx. 33</reference>. The wicked one shall be <hi type="italic">consumed with the breath of his mouth,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.8">2 Thess. ii. 8</reference>. (4.) He is of invincible strength and most terrible fierceness, so that he frightens all that come in his way, but is not himself frightened by any. Take a view of his neck, and there remains strength, <reference osisRef="Job.41.22">v. 22</reference>. His head and his body are well set together. <hi type="italic">Sorrow rejoices</hi> (or <hi type="italic">rides in triumph) before him,</hi> for he makes terrible work wherever he comes. Or, Those storms which are the sorrow of others are his joys; what is tossing to others is dancing to him. His flesh is well knit, <reference osisRef="Job.41.23">v. 23</reference>. <hi type="italic">The flakes</hi> of it <hi type="italic">are joined</hi> so closely <hi type="italic">together,</hi> and <hi type="italic">are so firm,</hi> that it is hard to pierce it; he is as if he were all bone. <hi type="italic">His flesh is of brass,</hi> which Job had complained his was not, <reference osisRef="Job.6.12">ch. vi. 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">His heart is as firm as a stone,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.41.24">v. 24</reference>. He has spirit equal to his bodily strength, and, though he is bulky, he is sprightly, and not unwieldy. As his flesh and skin cannot be pierced, so his courage cannot be daunted; but, on the contrary, he daunts all he meets and puts them into a consternation (<reference osisRef="Job.41.25">v. 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">When he raises up himself</hi> like a moving mountain in the great waters even <hi type="italic">the mighty are afraid</hi> lest he should overturn their ships or do them some other mischief. <hi type="italic">By reason of the breakings</hi> he makes in the water, which threaten death, <hi type="italic">they purify themselves,</hi> confess their sins, betake themselves to their prayers, and get ready for death. We read (<reference osisRef="Job.3.8">ch. iii. 8</reference>) of those who, when they raise up a leviathan, are in such a fright that they curse the day. It was a fear which, it seems, used to drive some to their curses and others to their prayers; for, as now, so then there were seafaring men of different characters and on whom the terrors of the sea have contrary effects; but all agree there is a great fright among them when the leviathan raises up himself. (5.) All the instruments of slaughter that are used against him do him no hurt and therefore are not error to him, <reference osisRef="Job.41.26-Job.41.29">v. 26-29</reference>. <hi type="italic">The sword</hi> and <hi type="italic">the spear,</hi> which wound nigh at hand, are nothing to him; the <hi type="italic">darts, arrows,</hi> and <hi type="italic">sling-stones,</hi> which wound at a distance, do him no damage; nature has so well armed him <hi type="italic">cap-a-pie—at all points,</hi> against them all. The defensive weapons which men use when they engage with the leviathan, as <hi type="italic">the habergeon,</hi> or breast-plate, often serve men no more than their offensive weapons; <hi type="italic">iron and brass</hi> are to him <hi type="italic">as straw and rotten wood,</hi> and he laughs at them. It is the picture of a hard-hearted sinner, that despises the terrors of the Almighty and laughs at all the threatenings of his word. The leviathan so little dreads the weapons that are used against him that, to show how hardy he is, he chooses to lie on the <hi type="italic">sharp stones, the sharp-pointed things</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.41.30">v. 30</reference>), and lies as easy there as if he lay on the soft mire. Those that would endure hardness must inure themselves to it. (6.) His very motion in the water troubles it and puts it into a ferment, <reference osisRef="Job.41.31-Job.41.32">v. 31, 32</reference>. When he rolls, and tosses, and makes a stir in the water, or is in pursuit of his prey, <hi type="italic">he makes the deep to boil like a pot,</hi> he raises a great froth and foam upon the water, such as is upon a boiling pot, especially <hi type="italic">a pot of</hi> boiling <hi type="italic">ointment;</hi> and <hi type="italic">he makes a path to shine after him,</hi> which even <hi type="italic">a ship in the midst of the sea</hi> does not, <reference osisRef="Prov.30.19">Prov. xxx. 19</reference>. One may trace the leviathan under water by the bubbles on the surface; and yet who can take that advantage against him in pursuing him? Men track hares in the snow and kill them, but he that tracks the leviathan dares not come near him. <div eID="gen10277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10278" type="x-p"/> 2. Having given this particular account of <hi type="italic">his parts, and his power, and his comely proportion,</hi> he concludes with four things in general concerning this animal:— (1.) That he is a non-such among the inferior creatures: <hi type="italic">Upon earth there is not his like,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.41.33">v. 33</reference>. No creature in this world is comparable to him for strength and terror. Or the earth is here distinguished from the sea: <hi type="italic">His dominion is not upon the earth</hi> (so some), but <hi type="italic">in the waters.</hi> None of all the savage creatures upon earth come near him for bulk and strength, and it is well for man that he is confined to the waters and there has <hi type="italic">a watch set upon him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.7.12">ch. vii. 12</reference>) by the divine Providence, for, if such a terrible creature were allowed to roam and ravage upon this earth, it would be an unsafe and uncomfortable habitation for the children of men, for whom it is intended. (2.) That he is more bold and daring than any other creature whatsoever: He <hi type="italic">is made without fear.</hi> The creatures are as they are made; the leviathan has courage in his constitution, nothing can frighten him; other creatures, quite contrary, seem as much designed for flying as this for fighting. So, among men, some are in their natural temper bold, others are timorous. (3.) That he is himself very proud; though lodged in the deep, yet <hi type="italic">he beholds all high things,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.41.34">v. 34</reference>. The rolling waves, the impending rocks, the hovering clouds, and the ships under sail with top and top-gallant, this mighty animal beholds with contempt, for he does not think they either lessen him or threaten him. Those that are great are apt to be scornful. (4.) <hi type="italic">That he is a king over all the children of pride,</hi> that is, he is the proudest of all proud ones. He has more to be proud of (so Mr. Caryl expounds it) than the proudest people in the world have; and so it is a mortification to the haughtiness and lofty looks of men. Whatever bodily accomplishments men are proud of, and puffed up with, the leviathan excels them and is a <hi type="italic">king over them.</hi> Some read it so as to understand it of God: <hi type="italic">He that beholds all high things, even he, is King over all the children of pride;</hi> he can tame the behemoth (<reference osisRef="Job.40.19">ch. xl. 19</reference>) and the leviathan, big as they are, and stout-hearted as they are. This discourse concerning those two animals was brought in to prove that it is God only who can <hi type="italic">look upon proud men and abase them, bring them low</hi> and <hi type="italic">tread them down,</hi> and <hi type="italic">hide them in the dust</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.40.11-Job.40.13">ch. xl. 11-13</reference>), and so it concludes with a <hi type="italic">quod erat demonstrandum—which was to be demonstrated;</hi> there is one that <hi type="italic">beholds all high things,</hi> and, wherein men deal proudly, is above them; he is <hi type="italic">King over all the children of pride,</hi> whether brutal or rational, and can make them all either bend or break before him, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.11">Isa. ii. 11</reference>. <hi type="italic">The lofty looks of man shall be humbled, and the haughtiness of men shall be bowed down, and</hi> thus <hi type="italic">the Lord alone shall be exalted.</hi>  <chapter eID="Job.41"/> <div eID="gen10278" type="x-p"/>

entries.c91a8706aab5f2081f9f459ece970e5a6a2d791f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5407"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 41</title> <div sID="gen8135" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Job.41.1-Job.41.34">Job 41:1-34</reference>.<div eID="gen8135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8136" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5407"/><hi type="bold">1. leviathan--</hi>literally, "the twisted animal," gathering itself in folds: a synonym to the Thannin (<reference osisRef="Job.3.8">Job 3:8</reference>, Margin; see <reference osisRef="Ps.74.14">Psa 74:14</reference>; type of the Egyptian tyrant; <reference osisRef="Ps.104.26">Psa 104:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.27.1">Is 27:1</reference>; the Babylon tyrant). A poetical generalization for all cetacean, serpentine, and saurian monsters (see on <reference osisRef="Job.40.15">Job 40:15</reference>, hence all the description applies to no one animal); especially the crocodile; which is naturally described after the river horse, as both are found in the Nile.<div eID="gen8136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8137" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tongue ... lettest down?--</hi>The crocodile has no tongue, or a very small one cleaving to the lower jaw. But as in fishing the tongue of the fish draws the baited hook to it, God asks, Canst thou in like manner take leviathan? <div eID="gen8137" type="x-p"/>
entries.1d9e1105cf3e0d9bf18f8ab7ca6c4810de9b5e59: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5408"/><div sID="gen8138" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5408"/><hi type="bold">2. hook--</hi>rather, "a rope of rushes."<div eID="gen8138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8139" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thorn--</hi>rather, a "ring" or "hook." So wild beasts were led about when caught (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.29">Is 37:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.4">Eze 29:4</reference>); fishes also were secured thus and thrown into the water to keep them alive. <div eID="gen8139" type="x-p"/>
entries.73bce7a8c8b8cb67621a06064d78a380a8418dce: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5409"/><div sID="gen8140" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5409"/><hi type="bold">3. soft words--</hi>that thou mayest spare his life. No: he is untamable. <div eID="gen8140" type="x-p"/>
entries.3d81b77b3082cdb34f0ceb305a9813891426f119: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5410"/><div sID="gen8141" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5410"/>4. Can he be tamed for domestic use (so <reference osisRef="Job.39.10-Job.39.12">Job 39:10-12</reference>)? <div eID="gen8141" type="x-p"/>
entries.029033e5e155191682596078bd614156afb38613: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5411"/><div sID="gen8142" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5411"/><hi type="bold">5. a bird?--</hi>that is, tamed. <div eID="gen8142" type="x-p"/>
entries.bd016a90c78f17e244327a96b40616fa9e9f591b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5412"/><div sID="gen8143" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5412"/>6. Rather, "partners" (namely, in fishing).<div eID="gen8143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8144" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">make a banquet--</hi>The parallelism rather supports Umbreit, "Do partners (in trade) desire to purchase him?" So the Hebrew (<reference osisRef="Deut.2.6">De 2:6</reference>).<div eID="gen8144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8145" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">merchants--</hi>literally, "Canaanites," who were great merchants (<reference osisRef="Hos.12.7">Ho 12:7</reference>, Margin). <div eID="gen8145" type="x-p"/>
entries.82bb48ed9c27916902f4b36be59a23cf3cdeee15: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5413"/><div sID="gen8146" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5413"/>7. His hide is not penetrable, as that of fishes. <div eID="gen8146" type="x-p"/>
entries.4b3ad41bc05045427f075c6c8f885f01debddcc4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5414"/><div sID="gen8147" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5414"/>8. If thou lay ... thou wilt have reason ever to remember ... and thou wilt never try it again. <div eID="gen8147" type="x-p"/>
entries.f4d5b2e022270b25b696bfbf0581b3d06011a92c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5415"/><div sID="gen8148" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5415"/><hi type="bold">9. the hope--</hi>of taking him.<div eID="gen8148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8149" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cast down--</hi>with fear "at the (mere) sight of him." <div eID="gen8149" type="x-p"/>
entries.a05a574603e1bda8f6728e9900f8dcd050346ab6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5416"/><div sID="gen8150" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5416"/><hi type="bold">10. fierce--</hi>courageous. If a man dare attack one of My creatures (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.9">Ge 49:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.24.9">Nu 24:9</reference>), who will dare (as Job has wished) oppose himself (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.2">Psa 2:2</reference>) to Me, the Creator? This is the main drift of the description of leviathan. <div eID="gen8150" type="x-p"/>
entries.1503c4c9e031cf40871cd3179001052668ed614b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5417"/><div sID="gen8151" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5417"/><hi type="bold">11. prevented--</hi>done Me a favor first: anticipated Me with service (<reference osisRef="Ps.21.3">Psa 21:3</reference>). None can call Me to account ("stand before Me," <reference osisRef="Job.41.10">Job 41:10</reference>) as unjust, because I have withdrawn favors from him (as in Job's case): for none has laid Me under a prior obligation by conferring on Me something which was not already My own. What can man give to Him who possesses all, including man himself? Man cannot constrain the creature to be his "servant" (<reference osisRef="Job.41.4">Job 41:4</reference>), much less the Creator. <div eID="gen8151" type="x-p"/>
entries.50546e22590d2c303a448ed30093e0d194d5777d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5418"/><div sID="gen8152" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5418"/><hi type="bold">12. I will not conceal--</hi>a resumption of the description broken off by the digression, which formed an agreeable change.<div eID="gen8152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8153" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his power--</hi>literally, "the way," that is, true proportion or expression of his strength (so Hebrew, <reference osisRef="Deut.19.4">De 19:4</reference>).<div eID="gen8153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8154" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">comely proportion--</hi>literally, "the comeliness of his structure" (his apparatus: so "suit of apparel" <reference osisRef="Judg.17.10">Jud 17:10</reference>) [Maurer]. Umbreit translates, "his armor." But that follows after. <div eID="gen8154" type="x-p"/>
entries.7bc860c0f483d9cff6885f63c9503b680921f7de: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5419"/><div sID="gen8155" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5419"/><hi type="bold">13. discover--</hi>rather, "uncover the surface" of his garment (skin, <reference osisRef="Job.10.11">Job 10:11</reference>): strip off the hard outer coat with which the inner skin is covered.<div eID="gen8155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8156" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with--</hi>rather, "within his double jaws"; literally, "bridle"; hence that into which the bridle is put, the double row of teeth; but "bridle" is used to imply that none dare put his hand in to insert a bridle where in other animals it is placed (<reference osisRef="Job.41.4">Job 41:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.39.10">39:10</reference>). <div eID="gen8156" type="x-p"/>
entries.536893ce95adfb46fa21d00bce05a7fcf4f7014b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5420"/><div sID="gen8157" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5420"/><hi type="bold">14. doors of ... face--</hi>his mouth. His teeth are sixty in number, larger in proportion than his body, some standing out, some serrated, fitting into each other like a comb [Bochart]. <div eID="gen8157" type="x-p"/>
entries.d498045888a51d34898e796abda8dfc34166cbba: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5421"/><div sID="gen8158" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5421"/>15. Rather, his "furrows of shields" (as "tubes," "channels," see on <reference osisRef="Job.40.18">Job 40:18</reference>), are, &c., that is, the rows of scales, like shields covering him: he has seventeen such rows.<div eID="gen8158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8159" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shut up--</hi>firmly closed together. A musket ball cannot penetrate him, save in the eye, throat, and belly. <div eID="gen8159" type="x-p"/>
entries.18257e2677ac8cddd35d6ff52bfea26804c50f26: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5422"/><div sID="gen8160" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5422"/>18. Translate: "his sneezing, causeth a light to shine." Amphibious animals, emerging after having long held their breath under water, respire by violently expelling the breath like one sneezing: in the effort the eyes which are usually directed towards the sun, seem to flash fire; or it is the expelled breath that, in the sun, seems to emit light.<div eID="gen8160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8161" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eyelids of morning--</hi>The Egyptian hieroglyphics paint the eyes of the crocodile as the symbol for morning, because the eyes appear the first thing, before the whole body emerges from the deep [Horæ Hierogliphicæ 1.65. Bochart]. <div eID="gen8161" type="x-p"/>
entries.3ac792e1c1bf3740345d7f21eae052794ff3e866: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5423"/><div sID="gen8162" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5423"/><hi type="bold">19. burning lamps--</hi>"torches"; namely, in respiring (<reference osisRef="Job.41.18">Job 41:18</reference>), seem to go out. <div eID="gen8162" type="x-p"/>
entries.69255747c5189e3a0fade8f6b954609b0c7743d8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5424"/><div sID="gen8163" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5424"/><hi type="bold">20. seething--</hi>boiling: literally, "blown under," under which a fire is blown. <div eID="gen8163" type="x-p"/>
entries.7d6f1693c2044bd83d5ffa316bc7798642961b25: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5425"/><div sID="gen8164" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5425"/><hi type="bold">21. kindleth coals--</hi>poetical imagery (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.8">Psa 18:8</reference>). <div eID="gen8164" type="x-p"/>
entries.9b6f850e7db75048b4081d4b4e0580cbccd88bbb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5426"/><div sID="gen8165" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5426"/><hi type="bold">22. remaineth--</hi>abideth permanently. His chief strength is in the neck.<div eID="gen8165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8166" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sorrow--</hi>anxiety or dismay personified.<div eID="gen8166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8167" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is turned into joy--</hi>rather, "danceth," "exulteth"; wherever he goes, he spreads terror "before him." <div eID="gen8167" type="x-p"/>
entries.69d6aba37753f3c47818b81fe2997a705132b787: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5427"/><div sID="gen8168" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5427"/><hi type="bold">23. flakes--</hi>rather, "dewlaps"; that which falls down (Margin). They are "joined" fast and firm, together, not hanging loose, as in the ox.<div eID="gen8168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8169" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">are firm--</hi>Umbreit and Maurer, "are spread."<div eID="gen8169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8170" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in themselves--</hi>rather, "upon him." <div eID="gen8170" type="x-p"/>
entries.be2f790756ceabdc6dcac7d0fdee15a322c7b5ae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5428"/><div sID="gen8171" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5428"/><hi type="bold">24. heart--</hi>"In large beasts which are less acute in feeling, there is great firmness of the heart, and slower motion" [Bochart]. The nether millstone, on which the upper turns, is especially hard. <div eID="gen8171" type="x-p"/>
entries.3ecbb91a9f8aa26835825f98f35cd192811f2d19: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5429"/><div sID="gen8172" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5429"/><hi type="bold">25. he--</hi>the crocodile; a type of the awe which the Creator inspires when He rises in wrath.<div eID="gen8172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8173" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">breakings--</hi>namely, of the mind, that is, terror.<div eID="gen8173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8174" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">purify themselves--</hi>rather, "they wander from the way," that is, flee away bewildered [Maurer and Umbreit]. <div eID="gen8174" type="x-p"/>
entries.15a8cb1b4be1bdb49f6f8757e58050eb8ddc3d2a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5430"/><div sID="gen8175" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5430"/><hi type="bold">26. cannot hold--</hi>on his hard skin.<div eID="gen8175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8176" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">habergeon--</hi>coat of mail; avail must be taken by zeugma out of "hold," as the verb in the second clause: "hold" cannot apply to the "coat of mail." <div eID="gen8176" type="x-p"/>
entries.e3e04fa8fb4deee24dae58ab8920c74276c523af: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5431"/><div sID="gen8177" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5431"/><hi type="bold">27. iron ... brass--</hi>namely, weapons. <div eID="gen8177" type="x-p"/>
entries.f72bf4435509334498895953d2a077f0442f26c0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5432"/><div sID="gen8178" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5432"/><hi type="bold">28. arrow--</hi>literally, "son of the bow"; Oriental imagery (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.13">La 3:13</reference>; Margin).<div eID="gen8178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8179" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stubble--</hi>Arrows produce no more effect than it would to throw stubble at him. <div eID="gen8179" type="x-p"/>
entries.8f1f3b7990d9000cdd990089ca0ffa6095133518: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5433"/><div sID="gen8180" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5433"/><hi type="bold">29. Darts--</hi>rather, "clubs"; darts have been already mentioned (<reference osisRef="Job.41.26">Job 41:26</reference>). <div eID="gen8180" type="x-p"/>
entries.2cfe78330c21e3008f2729da34c3650ed4981906: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5434"/><div sID="gen8181" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5434"/><hi type="bold">30. stones--</hi>rather, "potsherds," that is, the sharp and pointed scales on the belly, like broken pieces of pottery.<div eID="gen8181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8182" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sharp-pointed things--</hi>rather, "a threshing instrument," but not on the fruits of the earth, but "on the mire"; irony. When he lies on the mire, he leaves the marks of his scales so imprinted on it, that one might fancy a threshing instrument with its sharp teeth had been drawn over it (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.27">Is 28:27</reference>). <div eID="gen8182" type="x-p"/>
entries.28f3d7b7371605b7e7c384eec6127f67cbd56eac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5435"/><div sID="gen8183" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5435"/>31. Whenever he moves.<div eID="gen8183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8184" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sea--</hi>the Nile (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.5">Is 19:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.3.8">Na 3:8</reference>).<div eID="gen8184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8185" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pot of ointment--</hi>the vessel in which it is mixed. Appropriate to the crocodile, which emits a musky smell. <div eID="gen8185" type="x-p"/>
entries.d8c6e93877edfa6642d4862210770801aee48b79: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5436"/><div sID="gen8186" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5436"/><hi type="bold">32. path--</hi>the foam on his track.<div eID="gen8186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8187" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hoary--</hi>as hair of the aged. <div eID="gen8187" type="x-p"/>
entries.b494acb0d00cc9902381f37f82eda36742cb287b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5437"/><div sID="gen8188" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5437"/><hi type="bold">33. who--</hi>being one who, &c. <div eID="gen8188" type="x-p"/>
entries.63fe9a048f2f05c587df43aa957cad04e7e29d75: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5438"/><div sID="gen8189" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5438"/><hi type="bold">34. beholdeth--</hi>as their superior.<div eID="gen8189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8190" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">children of pride--</hi>the proud and fierce beasts. So <reference osisRef="Job.28.8">Job 28:8</reference>; Hebrew, "sons of pride." To humble the pride of man and to teach implicit submission, is the aim of Jehovah's speech and of the book; therefore with this as to leviathan, the type of God in His lordship over creation, He closes. <chapter eID="Job.41"/>

entries.d3c9d2dbae194436894e771da4dc517f8ba4a654: <div eID="gen18111" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen18112" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18113" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18113" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18112" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18114" type="x-p"/> God's great power in the leviathan, of which creature he gives a very circumstantial description, vv. 1-34. <div eID="gen18114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18115" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen18115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18116" type="x-p"/> Canst thou draw out leviathan - We come now to a subject not less perplexing than that over which we have passed, and a subject on which learned men are less agreed than on the preceding. What is leviathan? The Hebrew word לויתן livyathan is retained by the Vulgate and the Chaldee. The Septuagint have, Αξεις δε δρακοντα; "Canst thou draw out the Dragon?" The Syriac and Arabic have the same. A species of whale has been supposed to be the creature in question; but the description suits no animal but the crocodile or alligator; and it is not necessary to seek elsewhere. The crocodile is a natural inhabitant of the Nile, and other Asiatic and African rivers. It is a creature of enormous voracity and strength, as well as fleetness in swimming. He will attack the largest animals, and even men, with the most daring impetuosity. In proportion to his size he has the largest mouth of all monsters. The upper jaw is armed with forty sharp strong teeth, and the under jaw with thirty-eight. He is clothed with such a coat of mail as cannot be pierced, and can in every direction resist a musket-ball. The Hebrew לוי levi תן ten signifies the coupled dragon; but what this is we know not, unless the crocodile be meant. <div eID="gen18116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18117" type="x-p"/> With a hook - That crocodiles were caught with a baited hook, at least one species of crocodile, we have the testimony of Herodotus, lib. ii., c. 70: Επεαν νωτον συος δελεασῃ περι αγκιστρον, μετιει ες μεσον τον ποταμον, κ. τ. λ. "They take the back or chine of a swine, and bait a hook with it, and throw it into the midst of the river; and the fisherman stands at some distance on the shore holding a young pig, which he irritates, in order to make it squeak. When the crocodile hears this he immediately makes towards the sound; and, finding the baited hook in his way, swallows it, and is then drawn to land, when they dash mud into his eyes, and blind him; after which he is soon despatched." <div eID="gen18117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18118" type="x-p"/> In this way it seems leviathan was drawn out by a hook: but it was undoubtedly both a difficult and dangerous work, and but barely practicable In the way in which Herodotus relates the matter. <div eID="gen18118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18119" type="x-p"/> Or his tongue with a cord - It is probable that, when the animal was taken, they had some method of casting a noose round his tongue, when opening his mouth; or piercing it with some barbed instrument. Thevenot says that in order to take the crocodile they dig holes on the banks of the river, and cover them with sticks. The crocodiles fall into these, and cannot get out. They leave them there for several days without food, and then let down nooses which they pitch on their jaws, and thus draw them out. This is probably what is meant here.
entries.ab63fb7b0b0fb3b4a768b2a806d2f1347629569c: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen18119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18120" type="x-p"/> Canst thou put a hook onto his nose? - Canst thou put a ring in his nose, and lead him about as thou dost thine ox? In the East they frequently lead thy oxen and buffaloes with a ring in their noses. So they do bulls and oxen in this country. <div eID="gen18120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18121" type="x-p"/> Bore his jaw through with a thorn? - Some have thought that this means, Canst thou deal with him as with one of those little fish which thou stringest on a rush by means of the thorn at its end? Or perhaps it may refer to those ornaments with which they sometimes adorned their horses, mules, camels, etc.
entries.177b1d1d95192facf0e562a5517875097a1f2b96: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen18121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18122" type="x-p"/> Will he make many supplications - There are several allusions in these verses to matters of which we know nothing.
entries.80375fe69104bf18ca3e695639cb66bd23445c24: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen18122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18123" type="x-p"/> Will he make a covenant - Canst thou hire him as thou wouldst a servant, who is to be so attached to thy family as to have his ear bored, that he may abide in thy house for ever? Is not this an allusion to the law, <reference osisRef="Exo.21.1-Exo.21.6">Exo 21:1-6</reference>?
entries.5140807e3a20c29db09c077c88c1a4f9e210ff89: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen18123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18124" type="x-p"/> Wilt thou play with him - Is he such a creature as thou canst tame; and of which thou canst make a pet, and give as a plaything to thy little girls? נערותיך naarotheycha; probably alluding to the custom of catching birds, tying a string to their legs, and giving them to children to play with; a custom execrable as ancient, and disgraceful as modern.
entries.a008c42758920d5fc6f3eccf45ad68c1d4b1163b: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen18124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18125" type="x-p"/> Shall thy companions make a banquet - Canst thou and thy friends feast on him as ye were wont to do on a camel sacrificed for this purpose? Or, canst thou dispose of his flesh to the merchants - to buyers, as thou wouldst do that of a camel or an ox? It is certain, according to Herodotus, lib. ii. c. 70, that they killed and ate crocodiles at Apollonople and Elephantis, in Egypt.
entries.7be3c5edee61d6152c30ebd3c93a2c5812017436: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen18125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18126" type="x-p"/> Canst thou fill his skin with barbed irons? - This refers to some kind of harpoon work, similar to that employed in taking whales, and which they might use for some other kinds of animals; for the skin of the crocodile could not be pierced. Herrera says that he saw a crocodile defend itself against thirty men; and that they fired six balls at it without being able to wound it. It can only be wounded under his belly.
entries.0b86cd0408716204334a02a33d2bf1f9c5d2db0f: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen18126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18127" type="x-p"/> Lay thine hand upon him? - Mr. Heath translates, "Be sure thou strike home. Mind thy blow: rely not upon a second stroke." Mr. Good translates: - "Make ready thy hand against him. <div eID="gen18127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18128" type="x-p"/> Dare the contest: be firm." <div eID="gen18128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18129" type="x-p"/> He is a dangerous animal; when thou attackest him, be sure of thy advantage; if thou miss, thou art ruined. Depend not on other advantages, if thou miss the first. Kill him at once, or he will kill thee.
entries.e5faea772aaf66d3643d956fce8a5637a3054fda: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen18129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18130" type="x-p"/> Behold, the hope - If thou miss thy first advantage, there is no hope afterwards: the very sight of this terrible monster would dissipate thy spirit, if thou hadst not a positive advantage against his life, or a place of sure retreat to save thine own.
entries.bf5be1a01bfc6a2d6a7e1d5ea8024acd82c3c2db: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen18130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18131" type="x-p"/> None is so fierce that dare stir him up - The most courageous of men dare not provoke the crocodile to fight, or even attempt to rouse him, when, sated with fish, he takes his repose among the reeds. The strongest of men cannot match him. <div eID="gen18131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18132" type="x-p"/> Who then is able - If thou canst not stand against the crocodile, one of the creatures of my hand, how canst thou resist me, who am his Maker? This is the use which God makes of the formidable description which he has thus far given of this terrible animal.
entries.f9b9b059b1ad08260b9f1f5fd9427b0bbea77734: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen18132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18133" type="x-p"/> Who hath prevented me - Who is it that hath laid me under obligation to him? Do I need my creatures? All under the heavens is my property.
entries.80fccc2cc16cc76aa6e94a057d9bbc0735391501: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen18133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18134" type="x-p"/> I will not conceal his parts - This is most certainly no just translation of the original. The Vulgate is to this effect: I will not spare him: nor yield to his powerful words, framed for the purpose of entreaty. <div eID="gen18134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18135" type="x-p"/> Mr. Good applies it to leviathan: - "I cannot be confounded at his limbs and violence; <div eID="gen18135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18136" type="x-p"/> The strength and structure of his frame." <div eID="gen18136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18137" type="x-p"/> The Creator cannot be intimidated at the most formidable of his own works: man may and should tremble; God cannot.
entries.4d5f2ce0857fa7ecbe4a34b3e7a215f8eb2e8481: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen18137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18138" type="x-p"/> Who can discover the face of his garment? - Who can rip up the hide of this terrible monster? Who can take away his covering, in order to pierce his vitals?
entries.b16007b69824b77d6978ab1fed69c76c4560e062: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen18138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18139" type="x-p"/> The doors of his face? - His jaws which are most tremendous.
entries.010092da8d63860ed6c07571d4ef8454f2f376d2: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen18139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18140" type="x-p"/> His scales are his pride - They are impenetrable, as we have already seen.
entries.70d90b9058fe000c45e9bb8733db111789d69299: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen18140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18141" type="x-p"/> One is so near to another - It has already been stated, that a musket-ball fired at him in any direction cannot make a passage through his scales.
entries.7785cfd1ccd8e9da3f82809dba79158f403c0086: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen18141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18142" type="x-p"/> By his neesings a light doth shine - It is very likely that this may be taken literally. When he spurts up the water out of his nostrils, the drops form a sort of iris or rainbow. We have seen this effect produced when, in certain situations and state of the atmosphere, water was thrown up forcibly, so as to be broken into small drops, which has occasioned an appearance like the rainbow. <div eID="gen18142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18143" type="x-p"/> The eyelids of the morning - It is said that, under the water, the eyes of the crocodile are exceedingly dull; but when he lifts his head above water they sparkle with the greatest vivacity. Hence the Egyptians, in their hieroglyphics, made the eyes of the crocodile the emblem of the morning. Ανατολην λεγοντες δυο οφθαλμους κροκοδειλου ζωογραφουσι. - Horapp. Egypt. Ieroglyph., lib. i., c. 65. This is a most remarkable circumstance, casts light on ancient history, and shows the rigid correctness of the picture drawn above. The same figure is employed by the Greek poets. Χρυσεας ἡμερας βλεφαρον. "The eyelid of the golden day." <div eID="gen18143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18144" type="x-p"/> Soph. Antig. ver. 103. Νυκτος αφεγγες βλεφαρον. "The darksome eyelid of the night." <div eID="gen18144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18145" type="x-p"/> Eurip. Phaeniss. ver. 553.
entries.bb8078c7c4cd4953ce8d7bdb323bb4d7bbfa5c19: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen18145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18146" type="x-p"/> Out of his mouth go burning lamps - Dr. Young, in his paraphrase, has a sensible note on this passage: - "This is nearer the truth than at first view may be imagined. The crocodile, according to naturalists, lying long under water, and being there forced to hold its breath, when it emerges, the breath long repressed is hot, and bursts out so violently, that it resembles fire and smoke. The horse does not repress his breath by any means so long, neither is he so fierce and animated; yet the most correct of poets ventures to use the same metaphor concerning him, volvit sub naribus ignem. By this I would caution against a false opinion of the boldness of Eastern metaphors, from passages ill understood."
entries.64506c72ae6143f7061e4e7df0d442e94cd39aaf: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen18146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18147" type="x-p"/> In his neck remaineth strength - Literally, "strength has its dwelling in his neck." The neck is the seat of strength of most animals; but the head and shoulders must be here meant, as the crocodile has no neck, being shaped nearly like a lizard. <div eID="gen18147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18148" type="x-p"/> And sorrow is turned into joy before him - ולפניו תדוץ דאבה ulephanaiv taduts deabah; "And destruction exulteth before him." This is as fine an image as can well be conceived. It is in the true spirit of poetry, the legitimate offspring of the genie createur. Our translation is simply insignificant.
entries.52ce269d3fccce43562f678c1e0e6c87d3106bdb: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen18148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18149" type="x-p"/> The flakes of his flesh - His muscles are strongly and firmly compacted.
entries.1628f43f0f2ece8dd30ef0dae8e89a5dcc022e4a: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen18149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18150" type="x-p"/> Hard as a piece of the nether millstone - Which is required to be harder than that which runs above.
entries.6c21616f5f8ecf7fa4b5f3c4c6810f18e6f5033a: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen18150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18151" type="x-p"/> By reason of breakings they purify themselves - No version, either ancient or modern, appears to have understood this verse; nor is its true sense known. The Septuagint have, "When he turns himself, he terrifies all the quadrupeds on the earth." The original is short and obscure: משברים יתחטאו mishshebarim yithchattau. Mr. Good takes the plural termination ים im, from the first word, of which he makes the noun ים yam, the sea, and thus translates it, "They are confounded at the tumult of the sea." In this I can find no more light than in our own. Mr. Heath has, "For very terror they fall to the ground." The translations of it are as unsatisfactory as they are various. I shall give both the verses from Coverdale: - <div eID="gen18151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18152" type="x-p"/> His herte is as harde as a stone; and as fast as the stythye (anvil) that the hammer man smyteth upon: when he goeth the mightiest off all are afrayed, and the waives hevy. The dull swell in the waters proclaims his advance; and when this is perceived, the stout-hearted tremble.
entries.0675b0767bf154df8a1bb3f010a72d907bce98b0: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen18152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18153" type="x-p"/> Habergeon - The hauberk, the Norman armor for the head, neck, and breast, formed of rings. See on <reference osisRef="Neh.4.16">Neh 4:16</reference> (note).
entries.cff44d760bae7e3f2c6f77523ef3436782225858: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen18153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18154" type="x-p"/> Darts are counted as stubble - All these verses state that he cannot be wounded by any kind of weapon, and that he cannot be resisted by any human strength. A young crocodile, seen by M. Maillet, twelve feet long, and which had not eaten a morsel for thirty-five days, its mouth having been tied all that time, was nevertheless so strong, that with a blow of its tail it overturned a bale of coffee, and five or six men, with the utmost imaginable ease! What power then must lodge in one twenty feet long, well fed, and in health!
entries.13b440c7b7f4881cc82e23fecc7db2bbca5ef329: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen18154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18155" type="x-p"/> Sharp stones are under him - So hard and impenetrable are his scales, that splinters of flint are the same to him as the softest reeds.
entries.45cda1594e7d79b09930da1557bdd26716140549: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen18155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18156" type="x-p"/> He maketh the deep to boil like a pot - This is occasioned by strongly agitating the waters at or near the bottom; and the froth which arises to the top from this agitation may have the appearance of ointment. But several travelers say that the crocodile has a very strong scent of musk, and that he even imparts this smell to the water through which he passes, and therefore the text may be taken literally. This property of the crocodile has been noticed by several writers.
entries.6bf88adf6951accce4ccfdf58b7dd65e7f311551: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen18156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18157" type="x-p"/> He maketh a path to shine after him - In certain states of the weather a rapid motion through the water disengages many sparks of phosphoric fire. I have seen this at sea; once particularly, on a fine clear night, with a good breeze, in a fast-sailing vessel, I leaned over the stern, and watched this phenomenon for hours. The wake of the vessel was like a stream of fire; millions of particles of fire were disengaged by the ship's swift motion through the water, nearly in the same way as by the electric cushion and cylinder; and all continued to be absorbed at a short distance from the vessel. Whether this phenomenon takes place in fresh water or in the Nile, I have had no opportunity of observing. <div eID="gen18157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18158" type="x-p"/> The deep to be hoary - By the frost and foam raised by the rapid passage of the animal through the water.
entries.d82c6b5a6d5b2612a2f62269b1ce857e24fe6698: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen18158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18159" type="x-p"/> Upon earth there is not his like - There is no creature among terrestrial animals so thoroughly dangerous, so exceedingly strong, and so difficult to be wounded or slain. <div eID="gen18159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18160" type="x-p"/> Who is made without fear - Perhaps there is no creature who is at all acquainted with man, so totally destitute of fear as the crocodile.
entries.b432db94f435130cadf57c8bcccd257def2895d7: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen18160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18161" type="x-p"/> He is a king over all the children of pride - There is no animal in the waters that does not fear and fly from him. Hence the Chaldee renders it, all the offspring of Fishes. Calmet says, that by the children of pride the Egyptians are meant; that the crocodile is called their king, because he was one of their principal divinities; that the kings of Egypt were called Pharaoh, which signifies a crocodile; and that the Egyptians were proverbial for their pride, as may be seen in <reference osisRef="Eze.32.12">Eze 32:12</reference>. And it is very natural to say that Job, wishing to point out a cruel animal, adored by the Egyptians, and considered by them as their chief divinity, should describe him under the name of king of all the children of pride. Houbigant considers the לויתן livyathan, the coupled dragon, to be emblematical of Satan: "He lifts his proud look to God, and aspires to the high heavens; and is king over all the sons of pride." He is, in effect, the governor of every proud, haughty, impious man. What a king! What laws! What subjects! Others think that Men are intended by the sons of pride; and that it is with the design to abate their pride, and confound them in the high notions they have of their own importance, that God produces and describes an animal of whom they are all afraid, and whom none of them can conquer. <div eID="gen18161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18162" type="x-p"/> After all, what is leviathan? I have strong doubts whether either whale or crocodile be meant. I think even the crocodile overrated by this description. He is too great, too powerful, too important, in this representation. No beast, terrestrial or aquatic, deserves the high character here given, though that character only considers him as unconquerably strong, ferociously cruel, and wonderfully made. Perhaps leviathan was some extinct mammoth of the waters, as behemoth was of the land. However, I have followed the general opinion by treating him as the crocodile throughout these notes; but could not finish without stating my doubts on the subject, though I have nothing better to offer in the place of the animal in behalf of which almost all learned men and critics argue, and concerning which they generally agree. As to its being an emblem either of Pharaoh or the devil, I can say little more than, I doubt. The description is extremely dignified; and were we sure of the animal, I have no doubt we should find it in every instance correct. But after all that has been said, we have yet to learn what leviathan is!  <chapter eID="Job.41"/> <div eID="gen18162" type="x-p"/>

entries.5a0444ccf292aaea1a86d3a972c00d476c9f0ca9: <reference osisRef="Job.41.1-Job.5.1">Job 41:1-5   1</reference>  Dost thou draw the crocodile by a hoop-net, <div eID="gen8750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8751" type="x-p"/> And dost thou sink his tongue into the line?!   2  Canst thou put a rush-ring into his nose, <div eID="gen8751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8752" type="x-p"/> And pierce his cheeks with a hook?   3  Will he make many supplications to thee, <div eID="gen8752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8753" type="x-p"/> Or speak flatteries to thee?   4  Will he make a covenant with thee, <div eID="gen8753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8754" type="x-p"/> To take him as a perpetual slave?   5  Wilt thou play with him as a little bird, <div eID="gen8754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8755" type="x-p"/> And bind him for thy maidens? <div eID="gen8755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8756" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Job.3.8">Job 3:8</reference>, לויתן signified the celestial dragon, that causes the eclipses of the sun (according to the Indian mythology, <hi type="italic">râhu</hi> the black serpent, and <hi type="italic">ketu</hi> the red serpent); in <reference osisRef="Ps.104.26">Psa 104:26</reference> it does not denote some great sea-saurian after the kind of the hydrarchus of the primeval world,<note placement="foot">Vid., Grässe, <hi type="italic">Beiträge</hi>, S. 94ff.</note> but directly the whale, as in the Talmud (Lewysohn, <hi type="italic">Zoologie des Talm</hi>. §178f.). Elsewhere, however, the crocodile is thus named, and in fact as תּנּין also, another appellation of this natural wonder of Egypt, as an emblem of the mightiness of Pharaoh (vid., on Psa 74:13.), as once again the crocodile itself is called in Arab. <hi type="italic">el - fir‛annu</hi>. The Old Testament language possesses no proper name for the crocodile; even the Talmudic makes use of קרוקתא = κροκόδειλος (Lewysohn, §271). לויתן is the generic name of twisted, and תנין long-extended monsters. Since the Egyptian name of the crocodile has not been Hebraized, the poet contents himself in תּמשׁך with making a play upon its Egyptian, and in Arab. <hi type="italic">tmsâḥ , timsâḥ ,</hi><note placement="foot">Herodotus was acquainted with this name (χάμψαι = κροκόδειλοι); thus is the crocodile called also in Palestine, where (as Tobler and Joh. Roth have shown) it occurs, especially in the river <hi type="italic">Damûr</hi> near <hi type="italic">Tantûra</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen8756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8757" type="x-p"/> Arabized name (Ew. §324, <hi type="italic">a</hi>). To wit, it is called in Coptic <hi type="italic">temsah</hi>, Hierogl. (without the <hi type="italic">art</hi>.) <hi type="italic">msuh</hi> (<hi type="italic">emsuh</hi>), as an animal that creeps “out of the egg (<hi type="italic">suh</hi>).”<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Les naturalistes</hi> - says Chabas in his <hi type="italic">Papyr. magique</hi>, p. 190 - <hi type="italic">comptent cinq espèces de crocodiles vivant dans le Nil, mais les hieroglyphes rapportent un plus grand nombre de noms déterminés par le signe du crocodile</hi>. Such is really the case, apart from the so-called land crocodile or σκίγκος (Arab. <hi type="italic">isqanqûr</hi>), the Coptic name of which, <hi type="italic">hankelf</hi> (according to Lauth <hi type="italic">ha . n . kelf</hi>, ruler of the bank), is not as yet indicated on the monuments. Among the many old Egyptian names for the crocodile, Kircher’s <hi type="italic">charuki</hi> is, however, not found, which reminds one of the Coptic <hi type="italic">karus</hi>, as κροκόδειλος of κρόκος, for κροκόδειλος is the proper name of the <hi type="italic">Lacerta viridis</hi> (Herod. ii. 69). Lauth is inclined to regard <hi type="italic">charuki</hi> as a fiction of Kircher, as also the name of the phoenix, αλλοη (vid., p. 562). The number of names of the crocodile which remain even without <hi type="italic">charuki</hi>, leads one to infer a great variety of species, and crocodiles, which differ from all living species, have also actually been found in Egyptian tombs; vid., Schmarda, <hi type="italic">Verbreitung der Thiere</hi>, i. 89.</note> <div eID="gen8757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8758" type="x-p"/> In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.41.1">Job 41:1</reference></hi>, Ges. and others falsely translate: Canst thou press its tongue down with a cord; השׁקיע does not signify <hi type="italic">demergere</hi> = <hi type="italic">deprimere</hi>, but <hi type="italic">immergere:</hi> canst thou sink its tongue into the line, i.e., make it bite into the hook on the line, and canst thou thus draw it up? <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.41.1">Job 41:1</reference></hi> then refers to what must happen in order that the משׁך of the <hi type="italic">msuh</hi> may take place. Herodotus (and after him Aristotle) says, indeed, ii. 68, the crocodile has no tongue; but it has one, only it cannot stretch it out, because the protruding part has grown to the bottom of the mouth, while otherwise the saurians have a long tongue, that can be stretched out to some length. In <reference osisRef="Job.41.2">Job 41:2</reference> the order of thought is the same: for first the Nile fishermen put a ring through the gills or nose of valuable fish; then they draw a cord made of rushes (σχοῖνον) through it, in order to put them thus bound into the river. “As a perpetual slave,” <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.41.4">Job 41:4</reference></hi> is intended to say: like one of the domestic animals. By צפּור, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.41.5">Job 41:5</reference></hi>, can hardly be meant צפּרת הכּרמים, the little bird of the vineyard, i.e., according to a Talmud. usage of the language, the golden beetle (<hi type="italic">Jesurun</hi>, p. 222), or a pretty eatable grasshopper (Lewysohn, §374), but, according to the words of Catullus, <hi type="italic">Passer deliciae meae puellae,</hi> the sparrow, Arab. <hi type="italic">‛asfûr</hi> - an example of a harmless living plaything (שׂחק בּ, to play with anything, different from <reference osisRef="Ps.104.26">Psa 104:26</reference>, where it is not, with Ew., to be translated: to play with it, but: therein).
entries.8b5450833d4e975f976818d756a2ed23c6dfa0a6: <reference osisRef="Job.41.6-Job.9.6">Job 41:6-9   6</reference>  Do fishermen trade with him, <div eID="gen8758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8759" type="x-p"/> Do they divide him among the Canaanites?   7  Canst thou fill his skin with darts, <div eID="gen8759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8760" type="x-p"/> And his head with fish-spears?   8  Only lay thy hand upon him <div eID="gen8760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8761" type="x-p"/> Remember the battle, thou wilt not do it again!   9  Behold, every hope becometh disappointment: <div eID="gen8761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8762" type="x-p"/> Is not one cast down even at the sight of him? <div eID="gen8762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8763" type="x-p"/> The fishermen form a guild (Arab. <hi type="italic">ṣunf , sunf</hi>), the associated members of which are called חבּרים (distinct from חברים). On כּרה על, vid., on Job 6:27. “When I came to the towns of the coast,” says R. Akiba, <hi type="italic">b. Rosch ha-Schana,</hi> 26 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, ”they called selling, which we call מכירה, כירה, there,” according to which, then, <reference osisRef="Gen.50.5">Gen 50:5</reference> is understood, as by the Syriac; the word is Sanscrito-Semitic, Sanscr. <hi type="italic">kri</hi>, Persic <hi type="italic">chirı̂den</hi> (<hi type="italic">Jesurun</hi>, p. 178). lxx ἐνσιτούνται, according to 2Ki 6:23, to which, however, עליו is not suitable. כּנענים are Phoenicians; and then, because they were the merchant race of the ancient world, directly traders or merchants. The meaning of the question is, whether one sells the crocodile among them, perhaps halved, or in general divided up. Further, <reference osisRef="Job.41.7">Job 41:7</reference> : whether one can kill it בּשׂכּות, with pointed missiles (Arab. <hi type="italic">shauke</hi>, a thorn, sting, dart), or with fish-spears (צלצל, so called from its whizzing, צלל, <hi type="italic">óáëëá</hi>). In <reference osisRef="Job.41.8">Job 41:8</reference> the accentuation is the right indication: only seize upon him - remember the battle, i.e., thou wilt be obliged to remember it, and thou wilt have no wish to repeat it. זכר .ti t is a so-called <hi type="italic">imperat. consec.:</hi> if thou doest it, thou wilt ... , Ges. §130, 2. תּוסף is the pausal form of תּוסף (once <hi type="italic">ôï͂óð</hi>, <reference osisRef="Prov.30.6">Pro 30:6</reference>), of which it is the original form. <div eID="gen8763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8764" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">suff</hi>. of תּוהלתּו refers to the assailant, not objectively to the beast (the hope which he indulges concerning it). נכזבה, <reference osisRef="Job.41.9">Job 41:9</reference>, is 3 <hi type="italic">praet.,</hi> like נאלמה, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.7">Isa 53:7</reference> (where also the participial accenting as <hi type="italic">Milra</hi>, occurs in Codd.); Fürst’s <hi type="italic">Concord</hi>. treats it as <hi type="italic">part.,</hi> but the participial form נקטלה, to be assumed in connection with it, along with נקטלה and נקטלת, does not exist. הגם, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.41.9">Job 41:9</reference></hi>, is, according to the sense, equivalent to הלא גם, vid., on Job 20:4. מראיו (according to Ges., Ew., and Olsh., <hi type="italic">sing.,</hi> with the plural <hi type="italic">suff.,</hi> without a <hi type="italic">plur</hi>. meaning, which is natural in connection with the primary form מראי; or what is more probable, from the <hi type="italic">plur</hi>. מראים with a <hi type="italic">sing</hi>. meaning, as פּנים) refers to the crocodile, and יטּל (according to a more accredited reading, יטּל = יוּטל) to the hunter to whom it is visible. <div eID="gen8764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8765" type="x-p"/> What is said in <reference osisRef="Job.41.6">Job 41:6</reference> is perfectly true; although the crocodile was held sacred in some parts of Egypt, in Elephantine and Apollonopolis, on the contrary, it was salted and eaten as food. Moreover, that there is a small species of crocodile, with which children can play, does not militate against Job 41:5. Everywhere here it is the creature in its primitive strength and vigour that is spoken of. But if they also knew how to catch it in very early times, by fastening a bait, perhaps a duck, on a barb with a line attached, and drew the animal to land, where they put an end to its life with a lance-thrust in the neck (Uhlemann, <hi type="italic">Thoth</hi>, S. 241): this was angling on the largest scale, as is not meant in Job 41:1. If, on the other hand, in very early times they harpooned the crocodile, this would certainly be more difficult of reconcilement with v. 31, than that mode of catching it by means of a fishing-hook of the greatest calibre with Job 41:1. But harpooning is generally only of use when the animal can be hit between the neck and head, or in the flank; and it is very questionable whether, in the ancient times, when the race was without doubt of an unmanageable size, that has now died out, the crocodile hunt (<reference osisRef="Job.7.12">Job 7:12</reference>) was effected with harpoons. On the whole subject we have too little information for distinguishing between the different periods. So far as the questions of Jehovah have reference to man’s relation to the two monsters, they concern the men of the present, and are shaped according to the measure of power which they have attained over nature. The strophe which follows shows what Jehovah intends by these questions.
entries.5407c95f8998313cacb253bb85cbce5709645dc1: <reference osisRef="Job.41.10-Job.11.10">Job 41:10-11 10</reference>  None is so foolhardy that he dare excite him! <div eID="gen8765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8766" type="x-p"/> And who is it who could stand before Me? 11  Who hath given Me anything first of all, that I must requite it? <div eID="gen8766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8767" type="x-p"/> Whatsoever is under the whole heaven is Mine. <div eID="gen8767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8768" type="x-p"/> One sees from these concluding inferences, thus applied, what is the design, in the connection of this second speech of Jehovah, of the reference to behêmoth and leviathan, which somewhat abruptly began in Job 40:15. If even the strength of one of God’s creatures admits no thought of being able to attack it, how much more should the greatness of the Creator deter man from all resistance! For no one has any claim on God, so that he should have the right of appearing before Him with a rude challenge. Every creature under heaven is God's; man, therefore, possesses nothing that was not God’s property and gift, and he must humbly yield, whether God gives or takes away. לא, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.41.10">Job 41:10</reference></hi>, is not directly equivalent to אין, but the clause is exclamatory. יעורנו <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi>, יעירנו <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi>, is the Palestine reading, the reverse the Babylonian; the authorized text (chiefly without a <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi>) is יעוּרנּוּ from עוּר in a transitive signification (ἐγείρειν), as שׁוּב, <reference osisRef="Job.39.12">Job 39:12</reference>, comp. Job 42:10.
