The meaning of הקדּימני is determined according to ואשׁלּם: to anticipate, viz., by gifts presented as a person is approaching the giver (Arab. <hi type="italic">aqdama</hi>). הוּא, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.41.11">Job 41:11</reference></hi>, is neutral, as <reference osisRef="Job.13.16">Job 13:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.15.9">Job 15:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.31.11">Job 31:11</reference>, Job 31:28. תּחת is virtually a subj.: that which is under ... . After these apparently epiphonematic verses (2 and 3), one might now look for Job’s answer. But the description of the leviathan is again taken up, and in fact hitherto it was only the invincibility of the animal that was spoken of; and yet it is not so described that this picture might form the exact pendent of the preceding.
entries.f2c55d662a2f311fe79ad86d1441174d95badb70: <reference osisRef="Job.41.12-Job.14.12">Job 41:12-14 12</reference>  I will not keep silence about his members, <div eID="gen8768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8769" type="x-p"/> The proportion of his power and the comeliness of his structure. 13  Who could raise the front of his coat of mail? <div eID="gen8769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8770" type="x-p"/> Into his double teeth-who cometh therein? 14  The doors of his face-who openeth them? <div eID="gen8770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8771" type="x-p"/> Round about his teeth is terror. <div eID="gen8771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8772" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> לו authorized by the Masora assumes an interrogative rendering: as to it, should I be silent about its members (לו at the head of the clause, as <reference osisRef="Lev.7.7-Lev.7.9">Lev 7:7-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.9.2">Isa 9:2</reference>), - what perhaps might appear more poetic to many. החרישׁ (once, <reference osisRef="Job.11.3">Job 11:3</reference>, to cause to keep silence) here, as usually: to be silent. בּדּיו, as Job 18:13. דּבר signifies the relation of the matter, a matter of fact, as דּברי, facts, <reference osisRef="Ps.65.4">Psa 65:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.105.27">Psa 105:27</reference>; Psa 145:5. חין (compared by Ew. with הין, a measure) signifies grace, χάρις (as synon. חסד), here delicate regularity, and is made easy of pronunciation from חנן, just as the more usual חן; the language has avoided the form חנן, as observed above. לבוּשׁ . clothing, we have translated “coat of mail,” which the Arab. <hi type="italic">libâs</hi> usually signifies; פּני לבוּשׁו is not its face’s covering (Schlottm.), which ought to be לבוּשׁ פּניו; but פּני is the upper or front side turned to the observer (comp. <reference osisRef="Isa.25.7">Isa 25:7</reference>), as Arab. <hi type="italic">wjh</hi>, (<hi type="italic">wag'h</hi>), <hi type="italic">si rem desuper spectes, summa ejus pars, si ex adverso, prima</hi> (Fleischer, <hi type="italic">Glossae</hi>, i. 57). That which is the “doubled of its mouth” (רסן, prop. a bit in the mouth, then the mouth itself) is its upper and lower jaws armed with powerful teeth. The “doors of the face” are the jaws; the jaws are divided back to the ears, the teeth are not covered by lips; the impression of the teeth is therefore the more terrible, which the substantival clause, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.41.14">Job 41:14</reference></hi> (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.39.20">Job 39:20</reference>), affirms. שׁנּיו <hi type="italic">gen. subjecti:</hi> the circle, ἓρκος, which is formed by its teeth (Hahn).
entries.435ec8292c41af7065baf2d461fadf6875bafa6c: <reference osisRef="Job.41.15-Job.17.15">Job 41:15-17 15</reference>  A pride are the furrows of the shields, <div eID="gen8772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8773" type="x-p"/> Shut by a rigid seal. 16  One joineth on to the other, <div eID="gen8773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8774" type="x-p"/> And no air entereth between them. 17  One upon another they are arranged, <div eID="gen8774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8775" type="x-p"/> They hold fast together, inseparably. <div eID="gen8775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8776" type="x-p"/> Since the writer uses אפיק both in the signif. <hi type="italic">robustus</hi>, <reference osisRef="Job.12.12">Job 12:12</reference>, and <hi type="italic">canalis</hi>, <reference osisRef="Job.40.18">Job 40:18</reference>, it is doubtful whether it must be explained <hi type="italic">robusta</hi> (<hi type="italic">robora</hi>) <hi type="italic">scutorum</hi> (as e.g., Ges.), or <hi type="italic">canales scutorum</hi> (Hirz., Schlottm., and others). We now prefer the latter, but so that “furrows of the shields” signifies the square shields themselves bounded by these channels; for only thus is the סגוּר, which refers to these shields, considered, each one for itself, suitably attached to what precedes. חותם צר is an <hi type="italic">acc</hi>. of closer definition belonging to it: closed is (each single one) by a firmly attached, and therefore firmly closed, seal. lxx remarkably ὥσπερ σμυρίτης λίθος, i.e., (emery (vid., Krause’s <hi type="italic">Pyrogeteles</hi>, 1859, S. 228). Six rows of knotty scales and four scales of the neck cover the upper part of the animal’s body, in themselves firm, and attached to one another in almost impenetrable layers, as is described in <reference osisRef="Job.41.7">Job 41:7</reference> in constantly-varying forms of expression (where יגּשׁוּ with <hi type="italic">Pathach</hi> beside <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi> is the correct reading), - a גּאוה, i.e., an equipment of which the animal may be proud. Umbr. takes גאוה, with Bochart, = גּוה, the back; but although in the language much is possible, yet not everything.
entries.18302339a1e0673949e9c0b2c8dded6061fe7762: <reference osisRef="Job.41.18-Job.21.18">Job 41:18-21 18</reference>  His sneezing sendeth forth light, <div eID="gen8776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8777" type="x-p"/> And his eyes are like the eyelids of the dawn; 19  Out of his mouth proceed flames, <div eID="gen8777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8778" type="x-p"/> Sparks of fire escape from him; 20  Out of his nostrils goeth forth smoke <div eID="gen8778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8779" type="x-p"/> Like a seething pot and caldron; 21  His breath kindleth coals, <div eID="gen8779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8780" type="x-p"/> And flames go forth out of his mouth. <div eID="gen8780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8781" type="x-p"/> That the crocodile delights to sun itself on the land, and then turns its open jaws to the sunny side, most Nile travellers since Herodotus have had an opportunity of observing;<note placement="foot">Dieterici, <hi type="italic">Reisebilder</hi>, i. 194: “We very often saw the animal lying in the sand, its jaws wide open and turned towards the warm sunbeams, while little birds, like the slender white water-wagtail, march quietly about in the deadly abyss, and pick out worms from the watery jaws.” Herodotus, ii. 68, tells exactly the same story; as the special friend of the crocodile among little birds, he mentions τὸν τροχῖλον (the sand-piper, <hi type="italic">Pluvianus Aegyptius</hi>).</note> and in connection therewith the reflex action of sneezing may occur, since the light of the sun produces an irritation on the retina, and thence on the vagus; and since the sun shines upon the fine particles of watery slime cast forth in the act of sneezing, a meteoric appearance may be produced. This delicate observation of nature is here compressed into three words; in this concentration of whole, grand thoughts and pictures, we recognise the older poet. עטשׁ is the usual Semitic word for “sneezing” (Synon. זרר   2Ki 4:35). תּהל shortened from תּהל, <reference osisRef="Job.31.26">Job 31:26</reference>, <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. of הלל. The comparison of the crocodile’s eyes with עפעפּי־שׁחר (as <reference osisRef="Job.3.9">Job 3:9</reference>, from עפעף, to move with quick vibrations, to wink, i.e., tremble), or the rendering of the same as εἶδος ἑωσφόρου (lxx), is the more remarkable, as, according to Horus, i. 68, two crocodile’s eyes are the hieroglyph<note placement="foot">The eyes of the crocodile alone by themselves are no hieroglyph: how could they have been represented by themselves as <hi type="italic">crocodile’s eyes?</hi> But in the Ramesseum and elsewhere the crocodile appears with a head pointing upwards in company with couching lions, and the <hi type="italic">eyes</hi> of the crocodile are rendered specially prominent. Near this group it appears again in a curved position, and quite small, but this time in company with a scorpion which bears a disc of the sun. The former (κροκοδείλου δύο ὀφθαλμοί) seems to me to be a figure of the longest night, the latter (κροκόδειλος κεκυφώς in Horapollo) of the shortest, so that consequently ἀνατολή and δύσις do not refer to the rising and setting of the sun, but to the night as prevailing against or succumbing to the day (communicated by Lauth from his researches on the astronomical monuments). But since the growth of the day begins with the longest night, and <hi type="italic">vice versâ</hi>, the notions ἀνατολή and δύσις can, as it seems to me, retain their most natural signification; and the crocodile’s eyes are, notwithstanding, a figure of the light shining forth from the darkness, as the crocodile’s tail signifies black darkness (and Egypt as the black land).</note> for dawn, ἀνατολή: ἐπειδ́περ (probably to be read ἐπειδὴ πρὸ) παντὸς σώματος ζώου οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ ἐκ τοῦ βυθοῦ ἀναφαίνονται. There it is the peculiar brilliancy of the eyes of certain animals that is intended, which is occasioned either by the iris being furnished with a so-called lustrous substance, or there being in the pupil of the eye (as e.g., in the ostrich) that spot which, shining like metal, is called <hi type="italic">tapetum lucidum</hi>. For ἀναφαίνεσθαι of the eyes ἐκ τοῦ βυθοῦ, is the lustre of the pupil in the depth of the eye. The eyes of the crocodile, which are near together, and slanting, glimmer through the water, when it is only a few feet under water, with a red glow. <div eID="gen8781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8782" type="x-p"/> Nevertheless the comparison in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.41.18">Job 41:18</reference></hi> might also be intended differently. The inner (third) eyelid<note placement="foot">Prof. Will refers the figure not to the third eyelid or the <hi type="italic">membrana nictitans</hi>, but to that spot on the <hi type="italic">choroidea</hi>, glistening with a metallic lustre, which the crocodile has in common with most animals of the night or the twilight, therefore to the brilliancy of its eye, which shines by virtue of its lustrous coating; vid., the magnificent head of a crocodile in Schlegel’s <hi type="italic">Amphibien-Abbildungen</hi> (1837-44).</note> of the crocodile is itself a rose red; and therefore, considered in themselves, its eyes may also be compared with the “eyelids of the dawn.” What is then said, <reference osisRef="Job.41.19">Job 41:19</reference>, of the crocodile, Achilles Tatius, iv. 2, says of the hippopotamus: μυκτὴρ ἐπὶ μέγα κεχῃνὼς καὶ πνέων πυρώδη καπνὸν ὡς ἀπὸ πηγῆς πυρός. Bartram has observed on the alligator, that as it comes on the land a thick smoke issues from its distended nostrils with a thundering sound. This thick, hot steam, according to the credible description which is presented here, produces the impression of a fire existing beneath, and bursting forth. The subjective truth of this impression is faithfully but poetically reproduced by the poet. On כּידוד (root כד, <hi type="italic">escudere</hi>). התמלּט signifies no more than to disentangle one’s self, here therefore: to fly out in small particles. אגמון, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.41.19">Job 41:19</reference></hi>, is rendered by Saad., Gecat., and others, by <hi type="italic">qumqum</hi> (קומקום), a caldron; the modern expositors derive it from אגם = <hi type="italic">agama</hi>, to glow, and understand it of a “heated caldron.” But the word signifies either heat or caldron; the latter signification, however, cannot be linguistically established; one would look for אגּן (Arab. <hi type="italic">iggâne</hi>, a copper Germ. <hi type="italic">Waschkessel</hi>). The noun אגמון signifies, <reference osisRef="Job.40.2">Job 40:2</reference>, the reed σχοῖνος, and in the Jerusalem Talmud, <hi type="italic">Sota</hi> ix. 12, some menial service (comp. Arab. <hi type="italic">ugum</hi>); Ew. rightly retains the former signification, like a pot blown upon, i.e., fired, heated, and beside it (in combination with it) reeds as fuel, which in themselves, and especially together with the steaming water, produce a thick smoke. The Waw is to be compared to the Arabic <hi type="italic">Waw concomitantiae</hi> (which governs the <hi type="italic">acc</hi>.).
entries.9542e46172f6c6310ad381a88a60f0f963da4420: Job 41:22-25 22  Great strength resteth upon his neck, <div eID="gen8782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8783" type="x-p"/> And despair danceth hence before him. 23  The flanks of his flesh are thickly set, <div eID="gen8783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8784" type="x-p"/> Fitting tightly to him, immoveable. 24  His heart is firm like stone, <div eID="gen8784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8785" type="x-p"/> And firm like the nether millstone. 25  The mighty are afraid of his rising up; <div eID="gen8785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8786" type="x-p"/> From alarm they miss their aim. <div eID="gen8786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8787" type="x-p"/> Overpowering strength lodges on its neck, i.e., has its abiding place there, and before it despair, prop. melting away, dissolution (דּאבה from דּאב, Arab. <hi type="italic">ḏ'b</hi> = דּוּב <hi type="italic">Hiph.,</hi> Arab. <hi type="italic">ḍ'b</hi> II, to bring into a loose condition, synon. חמס), dances hence, i.e., spring up and away (ידוּץ, Arab. <hi type="italic">jadisu</hi>, to run away), i.e., it spreads before it a despondency which produces terror, and deprives of strength. Even the pendulous fleshy parts (מפּלי), especially of its belly, hang close together, דבקוּ, i.e., they are not flabby, but fit to it, like a metal casting, without moving, for the skin is very thick and covered with thick scales; and because the digestive apparatus of the animal occupies but little space, and the scales of the back are continued towards the belly, the tender parts appear smaller, narrower, and closer together than in other animals. יצוּק here is not, as <reference osisRef="Job.27.2">Job 27:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.29.6">Job 29:6</reference>, the <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. of צוּק, but the <hi type="italic">part</hi>. of יצק, as also <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.41.24">Job 41:24</reference></hi>: its heart is firm and obdurate, as though it were of cast brass, hard as stone, and in fact as the nether millstone (פלח from פלח, <hi type="italic">falacha</hi>, to split, crush in pieces), which, because it has to bear the weight and friction of the upper, must be particularly hard. It is not intended of actual stone-like hardness, but only of its indomitable spirit and great tenacity of life: the activity of its heart is not so easily disturbed, and even fatal wounds do not so quickly bring it to a stand. משּׂמו from שׂת = שׂאת = שׂאת), primary form שׂאתּ, is better understood in the active sense: afraid of its rising, than the passive: of its exaltedness. אילים (according to another reading אלים) is not, with Ew., to be derived from איל (Arab. <hi type="italic">ı̂jal</hi>), a ram; but אילים <reference osisRef="Exod.15.15">Exo 15:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.13">Eze 17:13</reference> (comp. גּירים <reference osisRef="2Chr.2.16">2Ch 2:16</reference>, נירי <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.29">2Sa 22:29</reference>), אלים <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.11">Eze 31:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.21">Eze 32:21</reference>, and אוּלים <hi type="italic">Cheth</hi>. 2Ki 24:15, are only alternating forms and modes of writing of the participial adject., derived from אוּל (איל) first of all in the primary form <hi type="italic">awil</hi> (as גּר = <hi type="italic">gawir</hi>). The signif. assigned to the verb אול: to be thick = fleshy, which is said then to go over into the signif. to be stupid and strong (Ges. <hi type="italic">Handwörterb</hi>.), rests upon a misconception: <hi type="italic">âla</hi> is said of fluids “to become thick,” because they are condensed, since they go back, i.e., sink in or settle (Ges. correctly in <hi type="italic">Thes.: notio crassitiei a retrocendendo</hi>). The verb <hi type="italic">âla , ja'ûlu ,</hi> unites in itself the significations to go backward, to be forward, and to rule; the last two: <hi type="italic">anteriorem</hi> and <hi type="italic">superiorem esse</hi>, probably belong together, and אל signifies, therefore, a possessor of power, who is before and over others. התחטּא, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.41.25">Job 41:25</reference></hi>, has the signif., which does not otherwise occur, to miss the mark (from חטא, Arab. <hi type="italic">chaṭiya</hi>, to miss, <hi type="italic">opp</hi>. Arab. <hi type="italic">ṣâb</hi>, to hit the mark), viz., (which is most natural where אילים is the subject spoken of) since they had designed the slaughter and capture of the monster. שׁברים is intended subjectively, as תּבירא = פּחד <reference osisRef="Exod.15.16">Exo 15:16</reference>, Targ. II, and also as the Arab. <hi type="italic">thubûr</hi>, employed more in reference to the mind, can be used of pain.
entries.a55d546ec6fd22a7ff0bdf49c1b1afeae1cb70a7: Job 41:26-29 26  If one reacheth him with the sword-it doth not hold; <div eID="gen8787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8788" type="x-p"/> Neither spear, nor dart, nor harpoon. 27  He esteemeth iron as straw, <div eID="gen8788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8789" type="x-p"/> Brass as rotten wood. 28  The son of the bow doth not cause him to flee, <div eID="gen8789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8790" type="x-p"/> Sling stones are turned to stubble with him. 29  Clubs are counted as stubble, <div eID="gen8790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8791" type="x-p"/> And he laugheth at the shaking of the spear. משּׂיגהוּ, which stands first as <hi type="italic">nom. abs.,</hi> “one reaching him,” is equivalent to, if one or whoever reaches him, Ew. §357, <hi type="italic">c</hi>, to which בּלי תקוּם, it does not hold fast (בּלי with <hi type="italic">v. fin.,</hi> as Hos 8:7; Hos 9:16, <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi>), is the conclusion. חרב is instrumental, as Psa 17:13. מסּע, from נסע, Arab. <hi type="italic">nz‛</hi>, to move on, hasten on, signifies a missile, as Arab. <hi type="italic">minz‛a</hi>, an arrow, <hi type="italic">manz‛a</hi>, a sling. The Targ. supports this latter signification here (<hi type="italic">funda quae projicit lapidem</hi>); but since קלא, the handling, is mentioned separately, the word appears to men missiles in general, or the catapult. In this combination of weapons of attack it is very questionable whether שׁריה is a cognate form of שׁריון (שׁרין), a coat of mail; probably it is equivalent to Arab. <hi type="italic">sirwe</hi> (<hi type="italic">surwe</hi>), an arrow with a long broad edge (comp. <hi type="italic">serı̂je</hi>, a short, round, as it seems, pear-shaped arrow-head), therefore either a harpoon or a peculiarly formed dart.<note placement="foot">On the various kinds of Egyptian arrows, vid., Klemm. <hi type="italic">Culturgeschichte</hi>, v. 371f.</note> “The son of the bow” (and of the אשׁפּה, <hi type="italic">pharetra</hi>) is the arrow. That the ἁπ. γεγρ. תותח signifies a club (war-club), is supported by the Arab. <hi type="italic">watacha</hi>, to beat. כּידון, in distinction from חנית (a long lance), is a short spear, or rather, since רעשׁ implies a whistling motion, a javelin. Iron the crocodile esteems as תּבן, <hi type="italic">tibn</hi>, chopped straw; sling stones are turned with him into קשׁ. Such is the name here at least, not for stumps of cut stubble that remain standing, but the straw itself, threshed and easily driven before the wind (<reference osisRef="Job.13.25">Job 13:25</reference>), which is cut up for provender (<reference osisRef="Exod.5.12">Exo 5:12</reference>), generally dried (and for that reason light) stalks (e.g., of grass), or even any remains of plants (e.g., splinters of wood).<note placement="foot">The Egyptio-Arabic usage has here more faithfully preserved the ancient signification of the word (vid., Fleischer, <hi type="italic">Glossae</hi>, p. 37) than the Syro-Arabic; for in Syria cut but still unthreshed corn, whether lying in swaths out in the field and weighted with stones to protect it against the whirlwinds that are frequent about noon, or corn already brought to the threshing-floors but not yet threshed, is called <hi type="italic">qashsh</hi>. - Wetzst.</note> <div eID="gen8791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8792" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">plur</hi>. נחשׁבוּ, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.41.29">Job 41:29</reference></hi>, does not seem to be occasioned by תותח being conceived collectively, but by the fact that, instead of saying תותח וכידון, the poet has formed וכידון into a separate clause. Parchon’s (and Kimchi’s) reading תוחח is founded upon an error.
entries.88cbf98ce0c669d0401b79109f3c8bd46dfec663: <reference osisRef="Job.41.30-Job.34.30">Job 41:30-34 30</reference>  His under parts are the sharpest shards, <div eID="gen8792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8793" type="x-p"/> He spreadeth a threshing sledge upon the mire. 31  He maketh the deep foam like a caldron, <div eID="gen8793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8794" type="x-p"/> He maketh the sea like a pot of ointment. 32  He lighteth up the path behind him, <div eID="gen8794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8795" type="x-p"/> One taketh the water-flood for hoary hair. 33  Upon earth there is not his equal, <div eID="gen8795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8796" type="x-p"/> That is created without fear. 34  He looketh upon everything high, <div eID="gen8796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8797" type="x-p"/> He is the king over every proud beast. <div eID="gen8797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8798" type="x-p"/> Under it, or, תּחתּיו taken like תּחת, <reference osisRef="Job.41.11">Job 41:11</reference>, as a virtual subject (vid., <reference osisRef="Job.28.5">Job 28:5</reference>): its under parts are the most pointed or sharpest shards, i.e., it is furnished with exceedingly pointed scales. חדּוּד is the intensive form of חד (Arab. <hi type="italic">hadı̂d</hi>, sharpened = iron, p. 542, note), as חלּוּק,   <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.40">1Sa 17:40</reference>, of חלק (smooth),<note placement="foot">In Arabic also this substantival form is intensive, e.g., <hi type="italic">lebbûn</hi>, an exceedingly large kind of tile, dried in the open air, of which farm-yards are built, nearly eight times larger than the common tile, which is called <hi type="italic">libne</hi> (לבנח).</note> and the combination חדּוּדי חרשׂ (equal the combination חדודי החרשׂים, comp. <reference osisRef="Job.30.6">Job 30:6</reference>) is moreover superlative: in the domain of shards standing prominent as sharp ones, as Arab. <hi type="italic">chairu ummatin ,</hi> the best people, prop. <hi type="italic">bon en fait de peuple </hi>(Ew. §313, <hi type="italic">c. Gramm. Arab</hi>. §532). lxx ἡ στρωμνὴ αὐτοῦ ὀβελίσκοι ὀξεῖς, by drawing ירפּד to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.41.30">Job 41:30</reference></hi>, and so translating as though it were רפידתו (Arab. <hi type="italic">rifâde , stratum</hi>). The verb רפד (<hi type="italic">rafada</hi>), cogn. רבד, signifies <hi type="italic">sternere</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.17.13">Job 17:13</reference>), and then also <hi type="italic">culcire;</hi> what is predicated cannot be referred to the belly of the crocodile, the scales of which are smooth, but to the tail with its scales, which more or less strongly protrude, are edged round by a shallow cavity, and therefore are easily and sharply separated when pressed; and the meaning is, that when it presses its under side in the morass, it appears as though a threshing-sledge with its iron teeth had been driven across it. <div eID="gen8798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8799" type="x-p"/> The pictures in <reference osisRef="Job.41.31">Job 41:31</reference> are true to nature; Bartram, who saw two alligators fighting, says that their rapid passage was marked by the surface of the water as it were boiling. With מצוּלה, a whirlpool, abyss, depth (from צוּל = צלל, to hiss, clash; to whirl, surge), ים alternates; the Nile even in the present day is called <hi type="italic">bahr</hi> (sea) by the Beduins, and also compared, when it overflows its banks, to a sea. The observation that the animal diffuses a strong odour of musk, has perhaps its share in the figure of the pot of ointment (lxx ὥσπερ ἐξάλειπτρον, which Zwingli falsely translates <hi type="italic">spongia</hi>); a double gland in the tail furnishes the Egyptians and Americans their (pseudo) musk. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.41.32">Job 41:32</reference></hi> the bright white trail that the crocodile leaves behind it on the surface of the water is intended; in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.41.32">Job 41:32</reference></hi> the figure is expressed which underlies the descriptions of the foaming sea with πολιός, <hi type="italic">canus</hi>, in the classic poets. שׂיבה, hoary hair, was to the ancients the most beautiful, most awe-inspiring whiteness. משׁלו, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.41.33">Job 41:33</reference></hi>, understood by the Targ., Syr., Arab. version, and most moderns (e.g., Hahn: there is not on earth any mastery over it), according to Zec 9:10, is certainly, with lxx, Jer., and Umbr., not to be understood differently from the Arab. <hi type="italic">mithlahu</hi> (its equal); whether it be an inflexion of משׁל, or what is more probable, of משׁל (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.17.6">Job 17:6</reference>, where this <hi type="italic">nomen actionis</hi> signifies a proverb = word of derision, and התמשּׁל, to compare one’s self, be equal, <reference osisRef="Job.30.19">Job 30:19</reference>). על־עפר is also Hebr.-Arab.; the Arabic uses <hi type="italic">turbe</hi>, formed from <hi type="italic">turâb</hi> (vid., on <reference osisRef="Job.19.25">Job 19:25</reference>), of the surface of the earth, and <hi type="italic">et - tarbâ - u</hi>as the name of the earth itself. העשׂוּ (for העשׂוּי, as צפוּ, <reference osisRef="Job.15.22">Job 15:22</reference>, <hi type="italic">Cheth</hi>. = צפוּי, resolved from עשׂוּו, <hi type="italic">‛asûw</hi>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.18">1Sa 25:18</reference>, <hi type="italic">Cheth</hi>.) is the confirmatory predicate of the logical subj. described in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.41.33">Job 41:33</reference></hi> as incomparable; and לבלי־חת (from חת, the <hi type="italic">a</hi> of which becomes <hi type="italic">i</hi> in inflexion), <hi type="italic">absque terrore</hi> (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.38.4">Job 38:4</reference>), is virtually a nom. of the predicate: the created one (becomes) a terrorless one (a being that is terrified by nothing). Everything high, as the לבלי־חת, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.41.33">Job 41:33</reference></hi>, is more exactly explained, it looketh upon, i.e., remains standing before it, without turning away affrighted; in short, it (the leviathan) is king over all the sons of pride, i.e., every beast of prey that proudly roams about (vid., on <reference osisRef="Job.28.8">Job 28:8</reference>).  <chapter eID="Job.41"/> <div eID="gen8799" type="x-p"/>

entries.45050e06233727744d40743fd163729c761fd5a6:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="41" type="chapter">
                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XLI.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1. CAnst thou draw out <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 span">
                           <ns0:desc>〈…〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:note> Leviathan with an hook? or his tongue with a cord <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 span">
                           <ns0:desc>〈…〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>which</ns0:hi> thou lettest down <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Canst thou take him with a Hook and a Line, as Anglers take ordinary Fishes? Surely no. <ns0:hi>Quest.</ns0:hi> What is this Leviathan? <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> This is granted on all hands, that it is a great and terrible Monster living in the Sea or Rivers, as <ns0:hi>Behemoth</ns0:hi> is a Land-monster. It is the general and received Opinion that it is the Whale, which is unquestionably called the <ns0:hi>Leviathan,</ns0:hi> Psal. 104. 25, 26. which having been discovered in the Seas next bordering upon <ns0:hi>Arabia</ns0:hi> probably was not unknown to <ns0:hi>Iob,</ns0:hi> who was a very inquisitive Person and well studied in the works of God, as this Book mani<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fests. But some later and very learned Interpreters conceive that it is the Crocodile; which was very well known in <ns0:hi>Egypt</ns0:hi> and all the parts adjacent to it. And this is evident, that the Hebrew word <ns0:hi>Thannin</ns0:hi> (which is Parallel to this word <ns0:hi>Leviathan,</ns0:hi> these two words being synonymous and the one promiscuously used for the other, as appears from <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 74. 13, 14. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 27. 1. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 32. 2.) is used of the <ns0:hi>Crocodile, Ezek.</ns0:hi> 29 3, 4. & 32. 2, 3. But I shall not positive<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly determine this Controversy; but onely shew how far the Text may be understood of both of them, and then submit it to the Readers Judgment, this being a matter of no great moment, wherein Christians may vary without any hazard. Onely this I will say, That whatever becomes of the <ns0:hi>Behemoth</ns0:hi> of the former Chapter, whether that be the Elephant, or the Hippopotamus, that doth not at all determine the sense of this <ns0:hi>Leviathan,</ns0:hi> but leaves it indifferent to the Whale or the Crocodile, as the context shall determine, which I confess seems to me to savour the latter more than the former. To which may be added, that it seems more probable that God would speak of such Creatures as were very well known to <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> and his Friends, as the Crocodile was, than of such as it is very uncertain whether they were known in those parts, and in <ns0:hi>Iob's</ns0:hi> time. This Verse, noting either the impossibi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lity, or rather the great and terrible difficulty, of taking this Mon<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ster with his Hook or Line, or such like instruments, may agree to either of them. For the Whale there is no doubt; nor much doubt as to the Crocodile; the taking whereof was generally esteemed by the Ancients to be very difficult and perillous; what<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />soever peculiar vertue or power from Nature or Art the <ns0:hi>Tentyritae</ns0:hi> had against them, as the <ns0:hi>Psylli</ns0:hi> were said to have against Serpents. Some indeed object, that the last Clause cannot agree to the Cro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />codile, because that hath no Tongue, as is affirmed by <ns0:hi>Aristotle, Pliny,</ns0:hi> and other ancient Authors. But that is a mistake and the ground of it is plain, because their Tongues are but small in propor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion to their vast Bodies, and withal fastned to their under Jaws, as the self-same Authors note. And that the Crocodile hath a tongue is positively affirmed by the said ancient Authors, and by the Hebrew Writers, and by the <ns0:hi>Arabians,</ns0:hi> to whom this Creature was best known, and by later Authors.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2. Canst thou put an hook <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Heb. a <ns0:hi>Bulrush,</ns0:hi> i. e. an Hook like a Bulrush with its head hang<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing down, as is expressed, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 58. 5.</ns0:note> into his nose <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">To hang him up by it for Sale, or to carry him home for use, after thou hast drawn him out of the Sea or River, of which he spake in the former Verse.</ns0:note>? or bore his jaw through with a thorn <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Or, with an Iron Hook or Instrument as sharp as a Thorn: wherewith thou usest to carry little Fishes.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3. Will he make many supplications unto thee? will he speak soft words unto thee <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Doth he dread thine anger or power? or will he humbly and earnestly beg thy favour, that thou wouldst spare him, and not pur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sue him, or release him out of Prison? It is a Metaphor from men in distress and misery who use these means to them to whose power they are subject.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4. Will he make a Covenant with thee <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">To wit, to do thee faithful service, as the next words explain it. Canst thou bring him into bondage and force him to serve thee?</ns0:note>? wilt thou take him for a servant for ever?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5. Wilt thou play with him as <ns0:hi>with</ns0:hi> a bird <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">As Children play with little Birds kept in Cages, or tied with strings; which they do at their pleasure and without any fear?</ns0:note>? or wilt thou bind him for thy maidens <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">For thy little Daughters; which he mentions rather than little Sons, because such are most subject to fear.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6. Shall the companions <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Thy Friends or Assistants in the taking of him.</ns0:note> make a banquet of him <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Feed upon him. Or, <ns0:hi>for him,</ns0:hi> i. e. for joy that thou hast taken him.</ns0:note>? shall they part him among the Merchants <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">As is usual in such cases, that all who are Partners in the labour and hazard may partake of the profit also and divide the spoil.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7. Canst thou fill his skin with barbed Irons, or his head with fish-spears <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">This may be understood, either 1. of the Whale. And whereas it is objected, that the Whales at this day are taken in this manner, and therefore this cannot be understood of them, it may be replied, both that this art and way of taking Whales is a late invention, and was not known in <ns0:hi>Iob's</ns0:hi> time, and that he doth not speak of the absolute impossibility, but of the great difficulty of taking them. Or 2. of the Crocodile, whose skin is so hard that an Iron or Spear will not pierce it, as we shall see hereafter.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8. Lay thine hand upon him <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Either, 1. in a familiar and friendly manner, that thou mayest catch him by deceit when thou canst not do it by force. Or rather 2. in way of Hostility, seize upon him and take him by a strong hand, if thou darest do so.</ns0:note>, remember the bat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tel <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">But ere thou do attempt that, consider what thou art doing and how hazardous thy enter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />prize is, and with whom, and with what disadvantage thou art going to fight, and as it follows, <ns0:hi>do no more,</ns0:hi> proceed no further, draw back thy hand, and be thankful for so great a deliverance. Or the Verse may be rendred thus. If (which Particle is oft understood) <ns0:hi>thou</ns0:hi> offer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />est or attemptest <ns0:hi>to lay</ns0:hi> violent <ns0:hi>hands on him thou wilt</ns0:hi> have cause to <ns0:hi>remember</ns0:hi> (the Imperative being put for the Future, which is frequent in the Hebrew Language) <ns0:hi>the battel,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>thou wilt do so no more;</ns0:hi> If thou doest escape, thou wilt never forget thy danger, nor attempt any thing of like nature for the time to come.</ns0:note>, do no more.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9. Behold, the hope of him <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Either, 1. of the Fish, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> the hope of taking or conquer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing him. Or, rather 2. of the Man who laid hands upon him as hoping to take him by force, but in vain.</ns0:note>, is in vain: shall not <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">The prefix <ns0:hi>He</ns0:hi> being put for <ns0:hi>Halo,</ns0:hi> as it is oft-times in the Hebrew Text, as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 27. 36. 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 2. 28. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 3. 6. & 31. 20. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 20. 30.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>one</ns0:hi> be cast down, even at the sight of him <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Not onely the fight, but the very fight of him is most frightful. Such is the sight of the Whale to Mariners, who fear the overturning of their Vessel. And such is the sight of the Crocodile, by which alone some have been affrighted out of their wits.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10. None <ns0:hi>is so</ns0:hi> fierce that dare stir him up <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">When he sleepeth or is quiet. None dare provoke him to the Battel.</ns0:note>: who then is able to stand before me <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">To contend with me his Creatour as thou <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> dost, when one of my Creatures is too hard for him.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:423" />11. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 11. 35 Psal. 24. 1. & 50. 12. 1 Cor. 10. 26.</ns0:note> who hath prevented me <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">To wit, with offices or service done for me, by which he hath laid the first obligation upon me, for which I am indebted to him. Who can be before-hand with me in kindnesses, since not onely the Leviathan, but all Men, and, as it follows, all things under Hea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven, are mine, made by my hand, and inriched with all their in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dowments by my favour, without which. O <ns0:hi>Iob,</ns0:hi> thou wouldst not have had either reason or speech to use so perversly to reproach my Providence. Having how said and largely proved that Man could not contend with God in power, he now adds, that he can<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />not do it in justice<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> because God oweth him nothing, nor is any way obliged to him. Which having briefly hinted to prevent an objection, he returns to his former argument the description of the Leviathan.</ns0:note> that I should re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pay <ns0:hi>him</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">That I should be ingaged to requite his favours</ns0:note>? <ns0:hi>whatsoever is</ns0:hi> under the whole heaven is mine <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Created by my power and favour, and wholly in my possession and at my dispose, and therefore cannot possibly prevent me, as was now said.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12. I will not conceal <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> I will particularly speak of them. Here is a <ns0:hi>Meiosis,</ns0:hi> as there is, Chap. 14. 11. & 15. 18. and oft elsewhere.</ns0:note> his <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. Chap. 18. 13.</ns0:note> parts <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>his bars,</ns0:hi> i. e. the Members of his Body which are strong like bars of Iron.</ns0:note>, nor his power, nor his comely proportion <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Which is more amiable and admirable in so vast a bulk.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13. Who can discover <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>uncover,</ns0:hi> or take off from him.</ns0:note> the face of his garment <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">The upper or outward part of his garment, or, the garment it self. the word <ns0:hi>face</ns0:hi> being oft redundant, as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 1. 2. & 23. 3. and oft elsewhere. And by the <ns0:hi>garment</ns0:hi> is meant the skin, which covers the whole Body, and may be taken off from the Body like a garment. Who dare at<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tempt to touch his very outward skin? much less dare any ven<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture to approach to him, to give him a deep or deadly wound.</ns0:note>? <ns0:hi>or</ns0:hi> who can come <ns0:hi>to him</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> within.</ns0:note> with his double bridle <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">To put it into his mouth and lead him by it to thy Stable and Service, as thou dost by an Horse. Or rather, (because he plainly seems to persist in describing the several parts of his Body: of which he speaks both in the foregoing and following words) <ns0:hi>Who can come within his double Bridle,</ns0:hi> to wit, his vast Jaws, which have some re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />semblance to a double Bridle: whence the Greeks call those parts of the face which reach to the Jaws on both sides, <ns0:hi>the Bridles.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14. Who can open the doors of his face <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">To wit, his Mouth. If it be open, none d<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>re enter within it, as he now said; and here he adds, that if it be shut, none dare open it.</ns0:note>? his teeth <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> terrible round about <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">This is true of some kinds of Whales, though others are said to have either none or no terrible teeth: but it is more eminently and unquestionably true of the Crocodile, of which this very thing is observed by all Authors who write of it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15. <ns0:hi>His</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> strong pieces of Shield.</ns0:note> scales <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> his pride <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">He prides and pleaseth himself in his strong and mighty scales. Heb. <ns0:hi>his strong shields</ns0:hi> (i. e. scales) are his <ns0:hi>pride.</ns0:hi> Or (as other both ancient and modern Interpreters render it) <ns0:hi>His body</ns0:hi> (or, <ns0:hi>His back,</ns0:hi> as this word is used, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 38. 17. which, if meant of the Crocodile, is emphatical, because his scales and strength is in his Back, where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />as his Eelly is very soft and easily pierced.) is <ns0:hi>the strength of shields,</ns0:hi> i. e. fortified with scales strong as Shields. This is meant either, 1. of the Whale, whose skin, though it be smooth and intire and without scales, may be said to be, as (which Particle is oft understood) <ns0:hi>strong shields,</ns0:hi> because it is, as <ns0:hi>Galen</ns0:hi> reports ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceeding hard and strong, and almost impenetrable and like a Shield, especially then when Shields were made of Leather; and so it is not onely on the back, as in the Crocodile, but also in the belly all over. Or, 2. of the Crocodile, which hath scales properly so called, and those most truely such as are here described, as all Authors and eye-witnesses consent.</ns0:note>, shut up together <ns0:hi>as with</ns0:hi> a close seal <ns0:hi>i.</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>p</ns0:hi> Closely compacted together, as things that are fastned together by a Seal.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16. One is so near to another <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Which plainly shews that the Shields or Scales are several; which agrees better to the Crocodile, than to the Whale, whose skin is all of one entire piece, unless there were a sort of Whales having thick and strong Scales; which some have affirmed, but is not yet known and proved.</ns0:note>, that no air can come between them.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17. They are joined one to another, they stick to<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gether, that they cannot be sundred <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">It is exceeding difficult and almost impossible by any power of art to so ever them one from another.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18. By his neesings <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Which may be understood, either, 1. of any commotion or agitation of the body like that which is in neezing, as when the Whale stirreth himself, and casteth or shooteth up great spours of water into the Air by the Pipes which God hath planted in his head for this use; which water being thin and transparent and illu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />minated by the Sun-beams casts forth a shining light. Or, 2. of neezing properly so called, which the Crocodile is said frequent<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly to do, because it commonly turneth its eyes to the Sun, as <ns0:hi>Stra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bo,</ns0:hi> and others note; which when a Man doth he is apt to neeze.</ns0:note> a light doth shine, and his eyes <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> like the eye lids of the morning <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">To which they seem very fitly compared, because the Eyes both of the Whale and Crocodile are dull and dark under the water, but as soon as they appear above water, they cast forth immediate<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly a bright and clear light, though not like that of the Sun at noon day, which had been too great an Hyperbole, yet like the Morn<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing light suddenly breaking forth after the dark Night.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19. Out of his mouth go burning Lamps <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> His breathings and blowings are very hot, or flaming, as the following Verses explains this. This also may seem better to agree to the Crocodile, which breaths (as <ns0:hi>Aristotle</ns0:hi> affirms) like the <ns0:hi>Hippopotamus,</ns0:hi> of which ancient Authors affirm, that <ns0:hi>his Noshils are very large, and he breaths forth a siery smoak like that of a Forna<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>,</ns0:hi> than to the Whale, which rather casts forth streams of Water, as was noted before, than flames of Fire, there being no such great heat observed in Whales, nor as far as I know, in any other fishes.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> sparks of fire leap out.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20. Out of his nostrils goeth smoak, <ns0:hi>as out</ns0:hi> of a seeth<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing pot or caldron <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>Pool.</ns0:hi> So a great Caldron is called, because it sends forth a great smoak as a Pool doth vapours; as in like manner the great brazen Laver in the Temple is called a <ns0:hi>S<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>a,</ns0:hi> for the great quantity of Water which it held.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21. His <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> breath kindleth Coals <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">An Hyperbolical Expression, noting onely extraordinary Heat.</ns0:note>, and a flame go<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth out of his Mouth.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22. In his neck remaineth strength <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">His Neck is exceeding strong. This is meant either 1. Of the Whale, who though he hath no Neck no more than other Fishes have, yet he hath a part in some sort answerable to it, where the Head and Body are joined together. Or 2. Of the Crocodile, whom <ns0:hi>Aristotle</ns0:hi> (who made it his business to search out the several Natures and Parts of all living Creatures, and had all the helps and advantages which he desired to find them out<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>) and <ns0:hi>Scaliger,</ns0:hi> and others, affirm to have a Neck, though some deny it.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> sorrow is turned into joy before him <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The approach of any Enemy, which usually causeth fear and sorrow in others, fills him with joy, as being desirous of nothing more than fighting. Or, <ns0:hi>sorrow rejoiceth,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>danceth,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>triumpheth,</ns0:hi> &c. <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> is prevalent and victorious, and quickly invades and conquers ail those Men, or other Creatures, which are in his way. Sorrow is his Companion, or Harbenger, which attends upon him where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />soever he goes. This may be a Po<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>tical Expression, like that of the Poets, when they bring in Anger and Fear going along with or before <ns0:hi>Mars</ns0:hi> into the Battle.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23. <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> The flakes <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>Parts,</ns0:hi> which stick out, or hang loose, and are ready to fall from other Fishes, or Creatures.</ns0:note> of his flesh <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">The word <ns0:hi>Flesh</ns0:hi> is used of Fishes also, as <ns0:hi>Lev.</ns0:hi> 11. 11. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 15. 39.</ns0:note> are joined together: they are firm in themselves, they cannot <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Without difficulty.</ns0:note> be moved <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">To wit, out of their place, or from the other Members of the Body.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24. His heart <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Either 1. That part of the Body is most firm, and hard, and strong. Or 2. His courage is invincible, he is void of fear for himself, and of compassion to others, which is oft called <ns0:hi>hard<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness of heart.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> is as firm as a stone, yea, as hard as a piece of the nether <ns0:hi>mill-stone</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Which being to bear the weight of the upper, ought to be the harder and stronger of the two.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25. When he raiseth up himself <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Shewing himself upon the top of the Waters. Or, <ns0:hi>
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> of his Height</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Greatness,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Majesty,</ns0:hi> for he is represented as a <ns0:hi>King, v.</ns0:hi> 34.</ns0:note>, the Mighty <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Even the stout hearted Mariners or Passengers, who use to be above fear.</ns0:note> are afraid: by reason of breakings <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Either 1. Of the Sea, caused by his motion<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> which dasheth the Waves in pieces one against another. Or rather 2. Of their Mind and State: by reason of their great danger and distress; which is expressed by this very word, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 60. 2. <ns0:hi>Ionah</ns0:hi> 2. 4.</ns0:note> they purifie them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Either 1. Naturally; that being the usual effect of great terrour. See <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 7. 17. Or rather 2. Morally, as this word is generally used. Those Mariners who ordinarily live in a gross and general neglect of God, and of Religion, are so affrighted with this imminent danger, that <ns0:hi>they <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>ry unto God in their trouble,</ns0:hi> as is said in like case, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 107. 28. and endeavour to purge their Consciences from the guilt of their sins, by confessing and seemingly forsaking of them, and to make their Peace with God, and obrain his favour and help, by their Vows, and Promises, and Prayers.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:423" />26. The Sword of him that layeth at him <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">That approacheth to him, and dare strike at him.</ns0:note> cannot hold <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>cannot stand, i. e.</ns0:hi> either 1. Cannot endure the stroke, but will be broken by it. Or rather 2. Cannot abide or take hold of him, or be fixed in him; but is instantly beaten back by the excessive hard<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness of the skin, which cannot be pierced by it, as may be gather<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed from this and other passages before and after it. This also seems better to agree to the Crocodile, whose skin no Sword, nor Dart, nor Musquet Bullet, (as others add) can pierce, than to the Whale, whose skin is easily pierced, as Experience sheweth in our Whales; except the Whale here spoken of were of another kind; which is not impossible.</ns0:note>: the spear, the dart, nor the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:note> habergeon <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Or, Breast-plate. As offensive Weapons cannot hurt him, so defensive Weapons cannot secure a Man from him. But men that go upon the design of taking either Whales or Crocodiles do not use to fortifie themselves in that manner. Some therefore take this to be another offensive Wea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pon, a kind of dart, as this word signifies in the <ns0:hi>Arabick</ns0:hi> Language; which is but a Dialect of the Hebrew, and from which the true signification of many Hebrew words must be gathered.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27. He esteemeth iron as straw <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">He neither fears nor feels the blows of the one more than of the other.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> brass as rotten wood.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28. The arrow <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>the son of the bow;</ns0:hi> as it is elsewere called <ns0:hi>the Son of the quiver,</ns0:hi> Lam. 3. 13. the Quiver being as it were the Mother or Womb that bears it, and the Bow as the Father that begers it or sendeth it forth.</ns0:note> cannot make him flee: sling-stones <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Great stones <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ast out of Slings, which have a great force and efficacy: of which see on 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 26. 14.</ns0:note> are turned with him into stubble <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Hurt him no more than a blow with a little stubble.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29. Darts are counted as stubble: he laugheth at the shaking of a spear <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">So far is he from fearing it, and fleeing from it, that he scorns and desies it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="30">30. <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Sharp. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> Sharp stones <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> under him: he spreadeth sharp-pointed things upon the mire <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">According to this Translation the sense is, His Skin is so hard and impenerable that the sharpest stones are as easie to him as the mire, and make no more impression upon him. But the words are and may be otherwise rendred as continuing the former sense, They (to wit, the Arrows, Darts or Stones cast at him) are, or fall <ns0:hi>under him,</ns0:hi> like (which Particle is oft understood) <ns0:hi>sharp shreads,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>frag<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments of stones, he spreadeth sharp pointed things</ns0:hi> (to wit, the pieces of Swords or Darts which were flung at him and broken upon him) <ns0:hi>upon the mire.</ns0:hi> The fragments of broken weapons lie as thick at the bot<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tom of the Water in the place of the fight, as little stones do in the mire, or as they do in a Field after some fierce and furious Battle. Or thus, <ns0:hi>with him</ns0:hi> (or <ns0:hi>for him,</ns0:hi> i. e. For his defence) <ns0:hi>are sharp stones, he spreadeth himself</ns0:hi> like <ns0:hi>an harrow,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>threshing instrument</ns0:hi> (which is fil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led and fortified with Iron) <ns0:hi>in the mire</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>mud</ns0:hi> in the bottom of the Water: So he doth not describe his resting-place, but rather his Back, which he not unfitly compares to sharp stones or threshing Instruments, because the Darts or Stones cast at him pierce no more into him than they would do into them if they were thrown at them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="31">31. He maketh the deep <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">The deep Waters, or the Sea, which is called <ns0:hi>the deep,</ns0:hi> Psal. 107. 24 <ns0:hi>Ionah</ns0:hi> 2. 3 as it is explained in the next Clause.</ns0:note> to boil like a pot <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">To swell, and foam, and froth by his strong and vehement motion, as any Liquor doth when it is boiled in a pot.</ns0:note>: he maketh the sea <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Either the great Sea, the proper place of the Whale, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 104. 25. or the great River <ns0:hi>Nilus,</ns0:hi> which is called <ns0:hi>a Sea,</ns0:hi> both in Scripture, as <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 11. 15. and in other Authors (of which see my Latin <ns0:hi>Synopsis</ns0:hi>) as <ns0:hi>Euphrates</ns0:hi> is called <ns0:hi>the Sea of Babylon,</ns0:hi> Isa. 21. 1. Jer. 51. 36. or Lakes or Pools, which are most frequently called <ns0:hi>Seas</ns0:hi> both in the Old and New Testament, as every one knows. And in such Lakes the Crocodiles are no less than in <ns0:hi>Nilus,</ns0:hi> as it is attested by <ns0:hi>Herodotus,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Strabo,</ns0:hi> and others.</ns0:note> like a pot of ointment <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">This Clause seems to be added very emphatically to intimate that this Leviathan causeth not onely a vehement commo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion, but also a great fragrancy in the Sea or Waters where it is. Which, though it was not observed by the Ancients, yet is unani<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mously affirmed by later Authors upon their own knowledge and experience, that it <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>asts a perfume like Musk; of which see the Names and Words of the Authors in my Latin <ns0:hi>Synopsis.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="32">32. He maketh a path to shine after him; <ns0:hi>one</ns0:hi> would think the deep <ns0:hi>to be</ns0:hi> hoary <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">When he raiseth himself to the top of the Waters, he doth as it were plow it up and make large furrows, and causeth a white froth or foam upon the Waters.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="33">33. Upon earth <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Either, 1. strictly so called as it is distinguished from the Sea or Rivers. There is no Land-creature comparable to him for strength and courage. Or 2. largely taken. No Creature equals him in all points. Or, <ns0:hi>upon the dust,</ns0:hi> as the word properly signifies, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Among all things that creep in the dust, among which this may in some sort be numbred for the shormess of its feet.                      <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">He doth not turn his back upon nor hide his face from the highest and proudest Creatures, but looks upon them with a bold and undaunted countenance, as being without any fear of them, as was now said.</ns0:note>: he <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> a king over all the children of pride. <ns0:note place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>z</ns0:hi> He carries himself with Princely Majesty and courage towards the stoutest and loftlest Creatures; which, though of far higher stature than himself, he striketh down with one stroke of his Tail, as he commonly doth Cows, and Horses, and sometimes Elephants.</ns0:note>
